questions.question: For a particle moving in a straight line, its displacement $x$ metres in terms of its velocity $v$ m/s is $x=8v-3\ln(v+2)$. The particle is initially moving at 1 m/s. Find the time $t$ seconds as a function of $v$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dx}{dv}=8-\dfrac{3}{v+2}=\dfrac{8v+13}{v+2}$. As $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=v$:

$$\frac{dt}{dv}=\frac1v\cdot\frac{dx}{dv}=\frac{8v+13}{v(v+2)}=\frac{13}{2v}+\frac{3}{2(v+2)}$$

$$t=\int_1^v\left(\frac{13}{2u}+\frac{3}{2(u+2)}\right)du=\frac{13}{2}\ln v+\frac32\ln\frac{v+2}{3}$$

questions.question: Using integration by parts, show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{1000}(1-x)^n\,dx=\frac{n}{1001}\int_0^1x^{1001}(1-x)^{n-1}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\left[\frac{x^{1001}}{1001}(1-x)^n\right]_0^1+\frac{n}{1001}\int_0^1x^{1001}(1-x)^{n-1}\,dx$, and the bracket vanishes at both limits (for $n\ge1$).

questions.question: Let $\displaystyle I_n=\int_0^1x^{1000}(1-x)^n\,dx$. Given $I_n=\dfrac{n}{1001+n}I_{n-1}$, show that $I_n=\dfrac{n!\,1000!}{(1001+n)!}$.
questions.answer:
$I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{1000}dx=\frac1{1001}$. Applying the relation repeatedly:
$$I_n=\frac{n}{1001+n}\cdot\frac{n-1}{1000+n}\cdots\frac{1}{1002}\cdot\frac{1}{1001}=\frac{n!\,1000!}{(1001+n)!}$$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{(n+1+x)^{n+1}}{(n+x)^n}$ for $x\ge0$, where $n\ge1$ is a fixed integer. Show that $f(x)$ is increasing for $x>0$.
questions.answer:
$$f'(x)=\frac{(n+1+x)^n}{(n+x)^{n+1}}\Big[(n+1)(n+x)-n(n+1+x)\Big]=\frac{x(n+1+x)^n}{(n+x)^{n+1}}>0$$
for $x>0$, so $f$ is increasing.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{(n+1+x)^{n+1}}{(n+x)^n}$ for $x\ge0$, where $n\ge1$ is a fixed integer. Given that $f$ is increasing for $x>0$, show that $\left(1+\dfrac{x}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}>\left(1+\dfrac xn\right)^n$ for $x>0$.
questions.answer:
$f(x)>f(0)$ gives
$$\frac{(n+1+x)^{n+1}}{(n+x)^n}>\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{n^n}$$
Rearranging (all terms positive): $\left(\dfrac{n+1+x}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}>\left(\dfrac{n+x}{n}\right)^n$.

questions.question: Let $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$. Show that the roots of $P(x)=0$ are among the roots of $x^9-1=0$.
questions.answer: $x^9-1=(x^3-1)(x^6+x^3+1)$, so every root of $P(x)=0$ is a root of $x^9-1=0$.

questions.question: Let $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$, whose roots are among the roots of $x^9-1=0$. Show that $P(x)=\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{9}+1\right)$.
questions.answer:
The roots of $x^9=1$ are $\text{cis}\dfrac{2k\pi}{9}$, $k=0,\pm1,\dots,\pm4$. Those with $k=0,\pm3$ are the roots of $x^3=1$, so the roots of $P$ are $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}9\right)$, $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{4\pi}9\right)$, $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{8\pi}9\right)$.

For each conjugate pair, $(x-\text{cis}\,\theta)(x-\text{cis}(-\theta))=x^2-2x\cos\theta+1$. Multiplying the three quadratics gives the factorisation (both sides are monic).

prev.question: Let $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$. Show that the roots of $P(x)=0$ are among the roots of $x^9-1=0$.
prev.answer: $x^9-1=(x^3-1)(x^6+x^3+1)$, so every root of $P(x)=0$ is a root of $x^9-1=0$.

questions.question: Given $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$ and $P(x)=\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{9}+1\right)$, evaluate $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}9\cos\dfrac{4\pi}9+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}9\cos\dfrac{8\pi}9+\cos\dfrac{2\pi}9\cos\dfrac{8\pi}9$.
questions.answer: Let the required sum be $S$. The coefficient of $x^2$ in the product is $3+4S$, and in $P(x)$ it is $0$. So $S=-\dfrac34$.

prev.question: Let $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$. Show that the roots of $P(x)=0$ are among the roots of $x^9-1=0$.
prev.answer: $x^9-1=(x^3-1)(x^6+x^3+1)$, so every root of $P(x)=0$ is a root of $x^9-1=0$.

prev.question: Let $P(x)=x^6+x^3+1$, whose roots are among the roots of $x^9-1=0$. Show that $P(x)=\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{9}+1\right)\left(x^2-2x\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{9}+1\right)$.
prev.answer:
The roots of $x^9=1$ are $\text{cis}\dfrac{2k\pi}{9}$, $k=0,\pm1,\dots,\pm4$. Those with $k=0,\pm3$ are the roots of $x^3=1$, so the roots of $P$ are $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}9\right)$, $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{4\pi}9\right)$, $\text{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{8\pi}9\right)$.

For each conjugate pair, $(x-\text{cis}\,\theta)(x-\text{cis}(-\theta))=x^2-2x\cos\theta+1$. Multiplying the three quadratics gives the factorisation (both sides are monic).

questions.question: Let $f$ be continuous for $a\le x\le b$. Show that $\displaystyle\left|\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\right|\le\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$-|f(x)|\le f(x)\le|f(x)|$ on $[a,b]$. Integrating,
$$-\int_a^b|f|\,dx\le\int_a^bf\,dx\le\int_a^b|f|\,dx$$
which is the required inequality.

questions.question: Using $\displaystyle\left|\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\right|\le\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx$, prove that $\displaystyle\left|\int_0^\pi27^x\cos x\,dx\right|\le\frac{3^{3\pi}-1}{3\ln3}$.
questions.answer: $$\left|\int_0^\pi27^x\cos x\,dx\right|\le\int_0^\pi27^x|\cos x|\,dx\le\int_0^\pi27^x\,dx=\left[\frac{27^x}{\ln27}\right]_0^\pi=\frac{3^{3\pi}-1}{3\ln3}$$

which is the required inequality.

questions.question: Given that $x_1+x_2>\sqrt{x_1x_2}$ for $x_1,x_2>1$, use mathematical induction to show that for all integers $n\ge2$, if $x_j>1$ for $j=1,\dots,n$, then $\ln(x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n)>\dfrac{1}{2^{n-1}}(\ln x_1+\ln x_2+\cdots+\ln x_n)$.
questions.answer:
**$n=2$:** taking logarithms of $x_1+x_2>\sqrt{x_1x_2}$ gives $\ln(x_1+x_2)>\frac12(\ln x_1+\ln x_2)$.

**Assume** $\ln(x_1+\cdots+x_k)>\dfrac1{2^{k-1}}(\ln x_1+\cdots+\ln x_k)$.

**$n=k+1$:** let $S=x_1+\cdots+x_k>1$. By the $n=2$ case applied to $S$ and $x_{k+1}$:
$$\ln(S+x_{k+1})>\tfrac12(\ln S+\ln x_{k+1})>\frac1{2^k}(\ln x_1+\cdots+\ln x_k)+\tfrac12\ln x_{k+1}$$
Since $\ln x_{k+1}>0$ and $\frac12\ge\frac1{2^k}$, the right side is at least $\dfrac1{2^k}(\ln x_1+\cdots+\ln x_{k+1})$.

So the result holds for $n=k+1$, and by induction for all $n\ge2$.

questions.question: A complex number $z$ is defined such that $|z - 1 + 2i| = 1$. Which of the following is the maximum modulus of $z$?
questions.answer: $z$ lies on the circle with centre $1 - 2i$ and radius 1. The maximum distance from the origin is $|1 - 2i| + 1 = \sqrt{5} + 1$.

questions.question: Which of the following is the magnitude of the vector $\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i} + \sin\theta\,\mathbf{j} + \tan\theta\,\mathbf{k}$, where $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$?
questions.answer: $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta + \tan^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \sec\theta$ (positive for $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$).

questions.question: Suppose John found a raven, and it was black. Which of the following **must** be false?
questions.answer:
Finding one black raven is consistent with all three statements: it does not show that non-black ravens exist, nor that they don't. None of A, B, C must be false, so the answer is D.

Note: the paper's answer key gives C, arguing that a non-black raven would disprove it — but no non-black raven was found, so "All ravens are black" is not shown to be false.
options: “There exist non-black ravens as well as black ravens.”

questions.question: The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, where $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$, $\overrightarrow{OB} = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{OC} = 3\mathbf{i} + a\mathbf{j} + b\mathbf{k}$. Which of the following are the values of $a$ and $b$?
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = 2\mathbf{i} + (a - 1)\mathbf{j} + b\mathbf{k} = \lambda\overrightarrow{AB}$ gives $\lambda = 2$, $a - 1 = -4$, $b = 2$: $a = -3$, $b = 2$.

questions.question: Let $z = \sqrt{3} + i$. Which of the following gives the geometric effect of multiplying the complex number $w$ by $\dfrac{\bar{z}}{z}$?
questions.answer: $z = 2\,\text{cis}\frac{\pi}{6}$, so $\frac{\bar{z}}{z} = \text{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$: modulus 1, a clockwise rotation by $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
options: $w$ is rotated anticlockwise by an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
$w$ is rotated anticlockwise by an angle of $\frac{2\pi}{3}$.
$w$ is rotated clockwise by an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
$w$ is rotated clockwise by an angle of $\frac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be true statements such that $A \Rightarrow B$. Which of the following statements is necessarily false?
questions.answer: $B$ is true, so $\sim B$ is false and "$A$ and $\sim B$" is false. (A is the contrapositive, which is true; C is true since $A$ is true.)

questions.question: It is given that $z = 1 + i$ is a root of $z^3 + bz^2 + 6z - 4 = 0$, where $b$ is a real number. Which of the following is the value of $b$?

The diagram shows a block at rest on a plane inclined at an angle $\theta$. The forces acting on the mass are gravitational, normal and frictional forces, as indicated (not to scale). Which of the following statements is always true?
questions.answer: At rest, resolving perpendicular and parallel to the plane: $N = mg\cos\theta \le mg$ and $F_f = mg\sin\theta \le mg$.

questions.question: Consider the integral $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{x^2 - 3x}e^{t^2}\,dt$, where $x$ is a variable limit. Which of the following values of $x$ minimises the integral?
questions.answer: The integrand $e^{t^2} > 0$, so the integral increases with its upper limit. It is smallest when $x^2 - 3x$ is smallest, at $x = \frac{3}{2}$. (Equivalently, $f'(x) = e^{(x^2 - 3x)^2}(2x - 3) = 0$ at $x = \frac{3}{2}$, changing from negative to positive.)

questions.question: Consider the complex numbers $a = 3 - 5i$ and $b = 2 + 3i$. Evaluate $a - \bar{b}$.
Solve for $z \in \mathbb{C}$: $z^2 + 2\bar{z} + 3 = 0$.
questions.answer:
Let $z = x + iy$: $x^2 - y^2 + 2x + 3 + i(2xy - 2y) = 0$.
Imaginary part: $2y(x - 1) = 0$, so $y = 0$ or $x = 1$.
- $y = 0$: $x^2 + 2x + 3 = 0$ has no real solutions.
- $x = 1$: $1 - y^2 + 2 + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow y = \pm\sqrt{6}$.

$z = 1 \pm \sqrt{6}\,i$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u = \tan x$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^4x\sec^4x\,dx$.
By using an appropriate substitution, find $\displaystyle\int x^3\sqrt{1 + x^2}\,dx$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 0$, and define $I_n = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}x^n\sin x\,dx$.

Show that $I_n = \pi^n - n(n - 1)I_{n-2}$ (for $n \ge 2$).
questions.answer:
By parts twice:
$$I_n = \left[-x^n\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} + n\int_0^{\pi}x^{n-1}\cos x\,dx = \pi^n + n\left(\left[x^{n-1}\sin x\right]_0^{\pi} - (n - 1)\int_0^{\pi}x^{n-2}\sin x\,dx\right) = \pi^n - n(n - 1)I_{n-2}.$$

questions.question: A particle has velocity equation $\dot{x}^2 = 4x - x^2$. Show that the particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: $\ddot{x} = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{2}\dot{x}^2\right) = 2 - x = -(x - 2)$, of the form $\ddot{x} = -n^2(x - c)$ with $n = 1$. So the motion is simple harmonic.

questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion with $\dot{x}^2 = 4x - x^2$ and $\ddot{x} = -(x - 2)$. Find the centre of motion, amplitude and period of the motion.
questions.answer: Centre $x = 2$. $\dot{x} = 0$ when $x(4 - x) = 0$, i.e. $x = 0, 4$, so the amplitude is 2. $n = 1$, so the period is $\frac{2\pi}{n} = 2\pi$.

prev.question: A particle has velocity equation $\dot{x}^2 = 4x - x^2$. Show that the particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion.

questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion with centre $x = 2$, amplitude 2 and $n = 1$. If the displacement is $x = 4$ at time $t = 0$, find the displacement $x$ as a function of time $t$.
questions.answer: It starts at the extreme $x = 4$: $x = 2 + 2\cos t$.

questions.question: On an Argand diagram, sketch the region representing the set of all $z$ satisfying $2 < |z| \le 4$ and $\frac{\pi}{6} \le \arg(z) < \frac{\pi}{3}$, showing the coordinates of any vertices.
questions.answer:
The region is the part of the annulus between radii 2 and 4 lying between the rays $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{6}$ and $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{3}$.
- Vertices: $2\,\text{cis}\frac{\pi}{6} = (\sqrt{3}, 1)$, $4\,\text{cis}\frac{\pi}{6} = (2\sqrt{3}, 2)$, $2\,\text{cis}\frac{\pi}{3} = (1, \sqrt{3})$, $4\,\text{cis}\frac{\pi}{3} = (2, 2\sqrt{3})$.
- Boundaries: outer arc $|z| = 4$ and ray $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{6}$ solid (included); inner arc $|z| = 2$ and ray $\arg z = \frac{\pi}{3}$ dashed (excluded).

questions.question: If $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are unit vectors such that $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, find the value of $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a}$.
questions.answer: $0 = |\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}|^2 = 3 + 2(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a})$, so the sum is $-\frac{3}{2}$.

questions.question: A sphere $\mathcal{S}_1$, with centre $C(2, 2, 2)$, passes through the point $A(4, 4, 4)$. Find the Cartesian equation of $\mathcal{S}_1$.

Sphere $\mathcal{S}_1$ has equation $(x - 2)^2 + (y - 2)^2 + (z - 2)^2 = 12$. A second sphere $\mathcal{S}_2$ has equation $(x - 2)^2 + (y - 2)^2 + (z - 5)^2 = 1$. Find the equation of the circle in which $\mathcal{S}_1$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ intersect.
questions.answer:
Subtracting: $(z - 2)^2 - (z - 5)^2 = 11 \Rightarrow 3(2z - 7) = 11 \Rightarrow z = \frac{16}{3}$.
Then $(x - 2)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 1 - \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{8}{9}$.
The circle is $(x - 2)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = \frac{8}{9}$ in the plane $z = \frac{16}{3}$ (centre $\left(2, 2, \frac{16}{3}\right)$, radius $\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$).

questions.question: Show that $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$.
questions.answer: $(a - b)^2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$.

questions.question:
It is known that $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$. Hence or otherwise, show that for all positive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$,
$$2(a^3 + b^3 + c^3) \ge ab(a + b) + bc(b + c) + ca(c + a).$$
questions.answer:
From $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$: $a^2 - ab + b^2 \ge ab$. Multiplying by $a + b > 0$: $a^3 + b^3 \ge ab(a + b)$.
Similarly $b^3 + c^3 \ge bc(b + c)$ and $c^3 + a^3 \ge ca(c + a)$. Adding the three gives the result.

prev.question: Show that $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$.
prev.answer: $(a - b)^2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$.

questions.question:
A particle is moving horizontally. Initially it is at the origin $O$ and moving with velocity 2 m s⁻¹. Its acceleration is $\ddot{x} = x - 2$, where $x$ is its displacement in metres at time $t$ seconds.

Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}^2 = (x - 2)^2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{2}v^2\right) = x - 2 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}v^2 = \frac{1}{2}(x - 2)^2 + C$. At $x = 0$, $v = 2$: $2 = 2 + C$, so $C = 0$ and $\dot{x}^2 = (x - 2)^2$.

questions.question:
A particle is moving horizontally. Initially it is at the origin $O$ and moving with velocity 2 m s⁻¹. Its acceleration is $\ddot{x} = x - 2$, where $x$ is its displacement in metres at time $t$ seconds. Its velocity satisfies $\dot{x}^2 = (x - 2)^2$.

Explain why $0 \le x < 2$ for all $t \in [0, \infty)$ and hence show that $\dot{x} = 2 - x$.
questions.answer:
The velocity can only be zero at $x = 2$, where $\ddot{x} = 0$ too: $x = 2$ is an equilibrium. The particle starts at $x = 0$ moving right ($v = 2 > 0$). While $x < 2$ its velocity cannot change sign, so it keeps moving right, and it cannot reach the equilibrium $x = 2$ in finite time (it approaches with speed $|x - 2| \to 0$). Hence $0 \le x < 2$ for all $t \ge 0$.
Then $\dot{x} > 0$ and $\dot{x} = |x - 2| = 2 - x$.

questions.question:
A particle is moving horizontally. Initially it is at the origin $O$ and moving with velocity 2 m s⁻¹. Its acceleration is $\ddot{x} = x - 2$, where $x$ is its displacement in metres at time $t$ seconds. Its velocity is $\dot{x} = 2 - x$.

Find an expression for $x$ as a function of $t$.
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\int_0^x\frac{dx}{2 - x} = \int_0^t dt \Rightarrow \ln\frac{2}{2 - x} = t \Rightarrow x = 2 - 2e^{-t}$.

questions.question: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Squares $ABPQ$ and $ACRS$ are erected on sides $AB$ and $AC$ as shown. Prove, using vector methods, that $|\overrightarrow{QS}| = 2|\overrightarrow{AM}|$.
questions.answer:
Let $\mathbf{b} = \overrightarrow{AB}$, $\mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{AC}$, $\mathbf{q} = \overrightarrow{AQ}$, $\mathbf{s} = \overrightarrow{AS}$, with $|\mathbf{q}| = |\mathbf{b}|$, $|\mathbf{s}| = |\mathbf{c}|$. The angles at $A$ total $360°$: $\angle QAS = 360° - 90° - 90° - \angle BAC = 180° - \angle BAC$. So
$$\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{s} = |\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}|\cos(180° - A) = -\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}.$$
Then $|\overrightarrow{QS}|^2 = |\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = |\mathbf{c}|^2 + |\mathbf{b}|^2 - 2\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{s} = |\mathbf{b}|^2 + |\mathbf{c}|^2 + 2\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c} = |\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}|^2$.
Since $\overrightarrow{AM} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c})$, $|\overrightarrow{QS}| = |\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}| = 2|\overrightarrow{AM}|$.

questions.question:
Consider the two perpendicular vectors $\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Find the unit vectors $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$.
questions.answer: $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(1, 2, 3)$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -2, 1)$.

questions.question:
Consider the two perpendicular vectors $\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Find a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ that is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
questions.answer: Let $\mathbf{w} = (p, q, r)$: $p + 2q + 3r = 0$ and $p - 2q + r = 0$. Subtracting: $4q + 2r = 0$, so $r = -2q$ and $p = 4q$. Taking $q = 1$: $(4, 1, -2)$, so $\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}(4, 1, -2)$ (or its negative).

questions.question: $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ are mutually perpendicular unit vectors. Let $\mathbf{x} = a\hat{\mathbf{u}} + b\hat{\mathbf{v}} + c\hat{\mathbf{w}}$, where $a, b, c$ are scalar constants. If $|\mathbf{x}| = 1$, prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$.
questions.answer: $1 = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x} = a^2(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}) + b^2(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}) + c^2(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}) + 2ab(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}) + \dots = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$, since each unit vector dotted with itself is 1 and the cross terms are 0.

questions.question: $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ are mutually perpendicular unit vectors, and $\mathbf{x} = a\hat{\mathbf{u}} + b\hat{\mathbf{v}} + c\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ with $|\mathbf{x}| = 1$. Let $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be the angles between $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\mathbf{x}$, $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ and $\mathbf{x}$, $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ respectively. Prove that $\cos\alpha + \cos\beta + \cos\gamma = a + b + c$.
questions.answer: $\cos\alpha = \dfrac{\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\mathbf{x}}{|\hat{\mathbf{u}}||\mathbf{x}|} = \hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\mathbf{x} = a$, using orthonormality. Similarly $\cos\beta = b$ and $\cos\gamma = c$. Adding gives the result.

prev.answer: $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(1, 2, 3)$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -2, 1)$.

prev.question:
Consider the two perpendicular vectors $\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Find a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ that is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
prev.answer: Let $\mathbf{w} = (p, q, r)$: $p + 2q + 3r = 0$ and $p - 2q + r = 0$. Subtracting: $4q + 2r = 0$, so $r = -2q$ and $p = 4q$. Taking $q = 1$: $(4, 1, -2)$, so $\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}(4, 1, -2)$ (or its negative).

prev.question: $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ are mutually perpendicular unit vectors. Let $\mathbf{x} = a\hat{\mathbf{u}} + b\hat{\mathbf{v}} + c\hat{\mathbf{w}}$, where $a, b, c$ are scalar constants. If $|\mathbf{x}| = 1$, prove that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$.
prev.answer: $1 = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x} = a^2(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}) + b^2(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}) + c^2(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}) + 2ab(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}) + \dots = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$, since each unit vector dotted with itself is 1 and the cross terms are 0.

questions.question: Given $\omega$ is a non-real root of $x^3 - 1 = 0$, show that $\omega$ is also a root of $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$.
questions.answer: $x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)$. Since $\omega^3 = 1$ and $\omega \ne 1$, $\omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0$.

questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a non-real cube root of unity, so $\omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0$. Hence prove by contradiction that $(x + 1)^{2n} + x^{2n} + 1$ is not divisible by $x^2 + x + 1$ if $n$ is divisible by 3.
questions.answer:
Suppose $n = 3m$ and $x^2 + x + 1$ divides $P(x) = (x + 1)^{2n} + x^{2n} + 1$. Since $\omega$ is a root of $x^2 + x + 1$, $P(\omega) = 0$.
But $\omega + 1 = -\omega^2$, so $(\omega + 1)^{6m} = \omega^{12m} = 1$, and $\omega^{6m} = 1$. Then $P(\omega) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \ne 0$, a contradiction. So $P(x)$ is not divisible by $x^2 + x + 1$.

prev.answer: $x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)$. Since $\omega^3 = 1$ and $\omega \ne 1$, $\omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0$.

questions.question:
Prove by mathematical induction that
$$\frac{1}{2} + \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta + \dots + \cos(n - 1)\theta = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{2n - 1}{2}\right)\theta}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}$$
for all $n \ge 2$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\theta \ne 2k\pi$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
questions.answer:
Key identity: $2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos k\theta = \sin\frac{(2k + 1)\theta}{2} - \sin\frac{(2k - 1)\theta}{2}$.

**$n = 2$:** RHS $= \dfrac{\sin\frac{3\theta}{2}}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} = \dfrac{\sin\frac{\theta}{2} + 2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\theta}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} = \frac{1}{2} + \cos\theta$ = LHS.

**Assume true for $n = k$.** Then for $n = k + 1$:
$$\text{LHS} = \frac{\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\theta}{2}}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} + \cos k\theta = \frac{\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\theta}{2} + \sin\frac{(2k + 1)\theta}{2} - \sin\frac{(2k - 1)\theta}{2}}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} = \frac{\sin\frac{(2k + 1)\theta}{2}}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}},$$
the required form for $n = k + 1$. Hence true for all $n \ge 2$ by mathematical induction.

questions.question:
Let $OABC$ be a convex quadrilateral where the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\overrightarrow{CO}$ correspond to the complex numbers $2a$, $2b$, $2c$ and $2d$ respectively, where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{C}$. The centres of the squares erected externally on each side of $OABC$ are $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ as shown in the diagram.

Show that $X$ is represented by the complex number $2a + b + ib$.
questions.answer: $A$ is $2a$ and the midpoint of $AB$ is $2a + b$. The centre $X$ of the square on $AB$ is half a side from this midpoint, perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and outwards (to the left of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, as $O \to A \to B \to C$ runs clockwise). That displacement is $i \times \frac{1}{2}(2b) = ib$. So $X = 2a + b + ib$.

questions.question:
Let $OABC$ be a convex quadrilateral where the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\overrightarrow{CO}$ correspond to the complex numbers $2a$, $2b$, $2c$ and $2d$ respectively, where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{C}$. The centres of the squares erected externally on each side of $OABC$ are $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ as shown in the diagram. It is known that $X = 2a + b + ib$.

Show that the line segments $WY$ and $XZ$ are equal in length and perpendicular.
questions.answer:
In the same way: $W = a + ia$, $Y = 2a + 2b + c + ic$, $Z = 2a + 2b + 2c + d + id$, and $a + b + c + d = 0$.
$$\overrightarrow{WY} = (a + 2b + c) + i(c - a).$$
$$\overrightarrow{XZ} = (b + 2c + d) + i(d - b) = (c - a) - i(a + 2b + c) \quad (\text{using } d = -a - b - c).$$
Then $i\,\overrightarrow{WY} = i(a + 2b + c) - (c - a) = -\overrightarrow{XZ}$. So $\overrightarrow{XZ}$ is $\overrightarrow{WY}$ rotated by $90°$ (times $-i$): they have equal length and are perpendicular.

questions.question: Consider the sequence given by $a_1 = 0$ and $a_n = \dfrac{1 + a_{n-1}}{2 + a_{n-1}}$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, $n \ge 2$. Prove, by mathematical induction, that $a_{n-1} < a_n$ for all integers $n \ge 2$.
questions.answer:
First, every term is non-negative: $a_1 = 0$, and if $a_{n-1} \ge 0$ then $a_n > 0$. Also
$$a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1 + a_n}{2 + a_n} - \frac{1 + a_{n-1}}{2 + a_{n-1}} = \frac{a_n - a_{n-1}}{(2 + a_n)(2 + a_{n-1})}.$$
**$n = 2$:** $a_2 = \frac{1}{2} > 0 = a_1$. True.
**Assume** $a_{k-1} < a_k$. Then $a_{k+1} - a_k = \dfrac{a_k - a_{k-1}}{(2 + a_k)(2 + a_{k-1})} > 0$, as the numerator and denominator are positive. So $a_k < a_{k+1}$.
Hence true for all $n \ge 2$ by mathematical induction.

questions.question:
Show that, for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $|x| < 1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^kx^k = \frac{1}{1 + x} - \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^{n+1}}{1 + x}.$$
questions.answer:
This is a geometric series with ratio $-x$ and $n + 1$ terms:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-x)^k = \frac{1 - (-x)^{n+1}}{1 + x} = \frac{1}{1 + x} - \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^{n+1}}{1 + x}.$$

questions.question: Prove that $0 \le \displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^{n+1}}{1 + x}\,dx \le \frac{1}{n + 2}$.
questions.answer:
For $0 \le x \le 1$, $1 + x \ge 1$, so $0 \le \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{1 + x} \le x^{n+1}$. Integrating over $[0, 1]$:
$$0 \le \int_0^1\frac{x^{n+1}}{1 + x}\,dx \le \int_0^1 x^{n+1}\,dx = \frac{1}{n + 2}.$$

questions.question:
It is known that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^kx^k = \frac{1}{1 + x} - \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^{n+1}}{1 + x}$ for $|x| < 1$, and $0 \le \displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^{n+1}}{1 + x}\,dx \le \frac{1}{n + 2}$. By integrating the first result and using the second, show that
$$\lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k + 1} = \ln 2.$$
questions.answer:
Integrating from 0 to 1 (both sides are continuous on $[0, 1]$):
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k + 1} = \ln 2 - (-1)^{n+1}\int_0^1\frac{x^{n+1}}{1 + x}\,dx.$$
By the squeeze theorem the integral tends to 0 as $n \to \infty$ (it lies between 0 and $\frac{1}{n + 2}$), so the sum tends to $\ln 2$.

questions.question: The equation $(z + i)^7 + (z - i)^7 = 0$ can be shown to have solutions satisfying $\dfrac{z + i}{z - i} = \text{cis}\left(\dfrac{(2m + 1)\pi}{7}\right)$ (do NOT prove this). Write down the set of values of $m$ for which the equation has distinct solutions, where $\dfrac{(2m + 1)\pi}{7} \in (-\pi, \pi]$.
questions.answer:
$-\pi < \frac{(2m + 1)\pi}{7} \le \pi \Rightarrow -4 < m \le 3$: $m \in \{-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$.
(The original uses exponential form $e^{i\theta}$; it is written here in cis form for the 2024 syllabus.)

questions.question: The solutions of $(z + i)^7 + (z - i)^7 = 0$ satisfy $\dfrac{z + i}{z - i} = \text{cis}\,2\theta$, where $\theta = \dfrac{(2m + 1)\pi}{14}$, $m \in \{-3, \dots, 3\}$. Given that $\dfrac{\text{cis}\,2\theta + 1}{\text{cis}\,2\theta - 1} = \dfrac{\text{cis}\,\theta + \text{cis}(-\theta)}{\text{cis}\,\theta - \text{cis}(-\theta)}$, show that the solutions can be written as $z = \cot\left(\dfrac{2m + 1}{14}\pi\right)$ for these values of $m$.
questions.answer:
$z + i = (z - i)\,\text{cis}\,2\theta \Rightarrow z(\text{cis}\,2\theta - 1) = i(\text{cis}\,2\theta + 1)$, so
$$z = i\cdot\frac{\text{cis}\,\theta + \text{cis}(-\theta)}{\text{cis}\,\theta - \text{cis}(-\theta)} = i\cdot\frac{2\cos\theta}{2i\sin\theta} = \cot\theta = \cot\left(\frac{2m + 1}{14}\pi\right).$$

questions.question: Using the binomial theorem, or otherwise, show that the non-zero roots of $(z + i)^7 + (z - i)^7 = 0$ are the roots of $z^6 - 21z^4 + 35z^2 - 7 = 0$.
questions.answer:
In the sum, the terms with odd powers of $i$ cancel:
$$(z + i)^7 + (z - i)^7 = 2\left[z^7 + \binom{7}{2}z^5i^2 + \binom{7}{4}z^3i^4 + \binom{7}{6}zi^6\right] = 2z\left(z^6 - 21z^4 + 35z^2 - 7\right).$$
So the non-zero roots are the roots of $z^6 - 21z^4 + 35z^2 - 7 = 0$.

The roots of $(z + i)^7 + (z - i)^7 = 0$ are $z = \cot\left(\frac{2m + 1}{14}\pi\right)$, $m = -3, \dots, 3$, and the non-zero roots are the roots of $z^6 - 21z^4 + 35z^2 - 7 = 0$. Hence show that
$$\sum_{k=0}^{2}\cot^2\left(\frac{2k + 1}{14}\pi\right) = 21.$$
questions.answer:
$m = 3$ gives $\cot\frac{\pi}{2} = 0$. The other six roots are $\pm\cot\frac{\pi}{14}$, $\pm\cot\frac{3\pi}{14}$, $\pm\cot\frac{5\pi}{14}$ (since $\cot(-x) = -\cot x$).

questions.question:
A projectile of mass $m$ is fired vertically upwards into a resistive medium, under gravity, with initial velocity $u$. After reaching its maximum height $H$, it falls freely back to the ground, vertically. The object experiences a resistive force $kv^2$ when travelling in both directions, where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion for the object falling is $m\dot{v} = mg - kv^2$.

Show that the terminal velocity $v_\tau$ that the object experiences when falling is $v_\tau = \sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{k}}$.
questions.answer: Terminal velocity when $\dot{v} = 0$: $mg - kv_\tau^2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_\tau = \sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{k}}$.

questions.question:
A projectile of mass $m$ is fired vertically upwards into a resistive medium, under gravity, with initial velocity $u$. After reaching its maximum height $H$, it falls freely back to the ground, vertically. The object experiences a resistive force $kv^2$ when travelling in both directions, where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion for the object falling is $m\dot{v} = mg - kv^2$. Its terminal velocity is $v_\tau = \sqrt{\frac{mg}{k}}$.

Show that the time $T$ at which the maximum height is reached is $T = \dfrac{v_\tau}{g}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{u}{v_\tau}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Going up (up positive), both forces act downwards: $m\dot{v} = -mg - kv^2$. With $k = \frac{mg}{v_\tau^2}$: $\dot{v} = -\frac{g}{v_\tau^2}(v_\tau^2 + v^2)$.
$$T = \int_0^u\frac{v_\tau^2}{g}\cdot\frac{dv}{v_\tau^2 + v^2} = \frac{v_\tau^2}{g}\cdot\frac{1}{v_\tau}\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{v_\tau} = \frac{v_\tau}{g}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{v_\tau}\right).$$

Hence show that the speed $W$ on impact with the ground is $W = \dfrac{u}{\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}}}$.
questions.answer:
Falling (down positive): $v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{g}{v_\tau^2}(v_\tau^2 - v^2)$. Over the fall of $H$:
$$\int_0^W\frac{v\,dv}{v_\tau^2 - v^2} = \frac{gH}{v_\tau^2} \Rightarrow -\frac{1}{2}\ln\left(1 - \frac{W^2}{v_\tau^2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(1 + \frac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}\right).$$
So $1 - \dfrac{W^2}{v_\tau^2} = \dfrac{v_\tau^2}{v_\tau^2 + u^2}$, giving $W^2 = \dfrac{u^2v_\tau^2}{v_\tau^2 + u^2} = \dfrac{u^2}{1 + \frac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}}$ and
$$W = \frac{u}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}}}.$$

prev.question:
A projectile of mass $m$ is fired vertically upwards into a resistive medium, under gravity, with initial velocity $u$. After reaching its maximum height $H$, it falls freely back to the ground, vertically. The object experiences a resistive force $kv^2$ when travelling in both directions, where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion for the object falling is $m\dot{v} = mg - kv^2$.

Show that the terminal velocity $v_\tau$ that the object experiences when falling is $v_\tau = \sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{k}}$.
prev.answer: Terminal velocity when $\dot{v} = 0$: $mg - kv_\tau^2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_\tau = \sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{k}}$.

prev.question:
A projectile of mass $m$ is fired vertically upwards into a resistive medium, under gravity, with initial velocity $u$. After reaching its maximum height $H$, it falls freely back to the ground, vertically. The object experiences a resistive force $kv^2$ when travelling in both directions, where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion for the object falling is $m\dot{v} = mg - kv^2$. Its terminal velocity is $v_\tau = \sqrt{\frac{mg}{k}}$.

Show that the time $T$ at which the maximum height is reached is $T = \dfrac{v_\tau}{g}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{u}{v_\tau}\right)$.
prev.answer:
Going up (up positive), both forces act downwards: $m\dot{v} = -mg - kv^2$. With $k = \frac{mg}{v_\tau^2}$: $\dot{v} = -\frac{g}{v_\tau^2}(v_\tau^2 + v^2)$.
$$T = \int_0^u\frac{v_\tau^2}{g}\cdot\frac{dv}{v_\tau^2 + v^2} = \frac{v_\tau^2}{g}\cdot\frac{1}{v_\tau}\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{v_\tau} = \frac{v_\tau}{g}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{v_\tau}\right).$$

prev.question:
A projectile of mass $m$ is fired vertically upwards into a resistive medium, under gravity, with initial velocity $u$. After reaching its maximum height $H$, it falls freely back to the ground, vertically. The object experiences a resistive force $kv^2$ when travelling in both directions, where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion for the object falling is $m\dot{v} = mg - kv^2$. Its terminal velocity is $v_\tau = \sqrt{\frac{mg}{k}}$.

Show that the maximum height $H$ is given by $H = \dfrac{v_\tau^2}{2g}\ln\left(1 + \dfrac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}\right)$.
prev.answer:
Going up: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -\dfrac{g}{v_\tau^2}(v_\tau^2 + v^2)$, so
$$H = \int_0^u\frac{v_\tau^2}{g}\cdot\frac{v\,dv}{v_\tau^2 + v^2} = \frac{v_\tau^2}{2g}\left[\ln(v_\tau^2 + v^2)\right]_0^u = \frac{v_\tau^2}{2g}\ln\left(1 + \frac{u^2}{v_\tau^2}\right).$$

questions.question: What is the value of $i^{2025}$?
A cubic polynomial $P(z)$ has all real coefficients. $z=3$ and $z=2+i$ are two roots of $P(z)=0$. Which equation describes $P(z)$?
questions.answer: The coefficients are real, so $2-i$ is also a root. The sum of the roots is $3+(2+i)+(2-i)=7$ so the coefficient of $z^2$ is $-7$, and the product is $3(2+i)(2-i)=15$ so the constant term is $-15$: $P(z)=z^3-7z^2+17z-15$ (B).

questions.question: Given that $z=\dfrac{\sqrt3+i}{1+i}$, which of the following is equal to $z^5$?
questions.answer: $\sqrt3+i=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi6$ and $1+i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$, so $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi6-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(-\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$. By de Moivre, $z^5=(\sqrt2)^5\operatorname{cis}\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)=4\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{19\pi}{12}$ (D).

questions.question: $ABCD$ is a rhombus with $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf b$. $BE$ is an extension of $AB$ such that $AB:BE=4:3$. The point $F$ is the midpoint of $CD$. Which expression gives the vector $\overrightarrow{FE}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$?
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{FC}=\dfrac12\overrightarrow{DC}=\dfrac12\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{BE}=\dfrac34\mathbf a$. So $\overrightarrow{FE}=\overrightarrow{FC}+\overrightarrow{CB}+\overrightarrow{BE}=\dfrac12\mathbf a-\mathbf b+\dfrac34\mathbf a=\dfrac54\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ (D).

questions.question: Which of the following Argand diagrams represents the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{Arg}(z-i)=\operatorname{Arg}(z+1)$? (Diagrams A–D are shown below in order.)
questions.answer: $z-i$ and $z+1$ are the vectors from $i$ and from $-1$ to $z$. They have the same argument only when they point the same way, so $z$ lies on the line through $-1$ and $i$ (gradient 1) outside the segment joining them. The points $-1$ and $i$ are excluded. Between them the vectors point in opposite directions. This is diagram A.

questions.question: A sign reads: "If you are not authorised, you may not enter." Which of the following statements is logically equivalent to it?
questions.answer: The sign is $\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q$, with $P$ = authorised and $Q$ = may enter. An implication is equivalent to its contrapositive, $Q\Rightarrow P$: "If you may enter, then you are authorised" (A). B and D are the converse.
options: If you may enter, then you are authorised.
If you are authorised, then you may enter.
If you are not authorised, then you may enter.
If you may not enter, then you are not authorised.

questions.question: A particle of unit mass is projected vertically upwards from the ground with initial velocity $u$ m/s. It is affected by gravity $g$ and a resistive force equivalent to $\dfrac12kv^2$, where the particle's velocity is $v$ m/s. Let $x$ be the displacement from the ground after $t$ seconds. Which of the following is the maximum height $H$ of the particle?
questions.answer: Going up, both gravity and resistance act downward, so $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\left(g+\dfrac k2v^2\right)$. Then $-\dfrac{v\,dv}{g+\frac k2v^2}=dx$. From the ground to the top, $x$ goes from $0$ to $H$ and $v$ goes from $u$ to $0$: $-\int_u^0\dfrac{v}{g+\frac{kv^2}2}dv=\int_0^H dx$. Reversing the limits, $H=\int_0^u\dfrac{v}{g+\frac{kv^2}2}dv$ (B).

questions.question: The curve $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2,t^4,t^6)$ is defined for all real values of $t$. Which of the following graphs best represents its projection onto the $xz$-plane? (Graphs A–D are shown below in order.)
questions.answer: With $x=t^2$ and $z=t^6$, $z=x^3$. Since $x=t^2\ge0$, only the half of the cubic with $x\ge0$ is traced (C).

questions.question: A car journey is split into two parts. During the first part the average speed is $V$ km/h and in the second part it is $U$ km/h. Kimie concludes that the average speed for the whole journey is $\dfrac{U+V}2$ km/h. Which of the following is NOT a counterexample to this conclusion?
questions.answer: A: 200 km in $5+2.5=7.5$ h, average $26.\dot6$ km/h, not 30, so it is a counterexample. B: 200 km in $2+2=4$ h, average 50 km/h $=\dfrac{60+40}{2}$, so the formula works and this is not a counterexample (B). (When equal times are spent at each speed the formula does hold.)
options: The car initially travels 100 km at 20 km/h, and then travels 100 km at 40 km/h.
The car initially travels 120 km at 60 km/h and 80 km at 40 km/h.
The car initially travels for one hour at 100 km/h and then two hours at 50 km/h.
The car initially travels 60 km in two hours and then travels 40 km in three hours.

questions.question: Consider the definite integral $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx$. Using the substitution $x=\pi-y$, what is the value of $I$?
questions.answer: $dx=-dy$; $x=0\to y=\pi$ and $x=\pi\to y=0$. $I=\int_\pi^0(\pi-y)\sin(\pi-y)(-dy)=\int_0^\pi(\pi-y)\sin y\,dy=\pi\int_0^\pi\sin y\,dy-I$. So $2I=\pi\int_0^\pi\sin y\,dy$ and $I=\dfrac\pi2\int_0^\pi\sin y\,dy$ (C).

questions.question: Let $z_1=-1-5i$ and $z_2=2-i$. Calculate $i(z_1-z_2)$.
Let $z_2=2-i$. Write $\dfrac{a+ib}{z_2}$ in the form $\omega=x+iy$, in terms of $a$ and $b$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{a+ib}{2-i}\times\dfrac{2+i}{2+i}=\dfrac{2a+ai+2bi-b}{5}=\dfrac{2a-b}{5}+\dfrac{a+2b}{5}i$.

prev.question: Let $z_1=-1-5i$ and $z_2=2-i$. Calculate $i(z_1-z_2)$.

questions.question: Consider the statement about integers: if $k^2-14k$ is odd, then $k$ is odd. By considering the contrapositive prove that the statement is true.
questions.answer: The contrapositive is: if $k$ is even, then $k^2-14k$ is even. Let $k=2M$ for an integer $M$. Then $k^2-14k=4M^2-28M=2(2M^2-14M)$, which is even because $2M^2-14M$ is an integer. The contrapositive is true, so the original statement is true.

questions.question: Let $P(x,y,z)$ be any point that is equidistant from $Q(2,-3,4)$ and $R(-7,1,0)$. Show that the equation of all such points $P$ is $18x-8y+8z=-21$.
The set of points $P(x,y,z)$ equidistant from $Q(2,-3,4)$ and $R(-7,1,0)$ satisfies $18x-8y+8z=-21$. Give a geometric description of $P$.
questions.answer: The points $P$ form a plane: the perpendicular bisector plane of the segment $QR$ (it passes through the midpoint of $QR$ and is perpendicular to $QR$).

prev.question: Let $P(x,y,z)$ be any point that is equidistant from $Q(2,-3,4)$ and $R(-7,1,0)$. Show that the equation of all such points $P$ is $18x-8y+8z=-21$.

questions.question: Solve $z^2+(5+5i)z+(6+15i)=0$. Give your answer in the form $z=x+iy$.
Use partial fractions to find $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^1\dfrac{1+7x}{(x-2)(x+3)}dx$.
Use mathematical induction to prove that if $S_1=a$ and $S_n-S_{n-1}=ar^{n-1}$, $n\ge2$, then $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$, $n\ge1$.
questions.answer:
Base case $n=1$: $\dfrac{a(1-r)}{1-r}=a=S_1$, so it is true for $n=1$.

Assume true for $n=k$: $S_k=\dfrac{a(1-r^k)}{1-r}$. Then for $n=k+1$, $S_{k+1}=S_k+ar^k=\dfrac{a(1-r^k)}{1-r}+ar^k=\dfrac{a(1-r^k)+ar^k(1-r)}{1-r}=\dfrac{a-ar^k+ar^k-ar^{k+1}}{1-r}=\dfrac{a(1-r^{k+1})}{1-r}$.

So if it is true for $n=k$ it is true for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all integers $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Consider the complex number $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Write $z$ in mod-arg form.
questions.answer: $|z|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$ and $\arg z=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\dfrac\pi3$, so $z=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi3$.

questions.question: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Show $\sqrt{z^3}=2\sqrt2\,i$.
questions.answer: $z^3=2^3\operatorname{cis}\pi=-8$, and $\sqrt{-8}=\sqrt8\,i=2\sqrt2\,i$.

prev.question: Consider the complex number $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Write $z$ in mod-arg form.
prev.answer: $|z|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$ and $\arg z=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\dfrac\pi3$, so $z=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi3$.

questions.question: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Find all values of $n$ for which $z^n$ is purely imaginary.
questions.answer: $z^n=2^n\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{n\pi}3$ is purely imaginary when $\cos\dfrac{n\pi}3=0$, i.e. $\dfrac{n\pi}3=\dfrac\pi2+k\pi$, so $n=\dfrac{6k+3}2=\dfrac32+3k$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. These values are never integers, so no integer power of $z$ is purely imaginary.

questions.question: Find the Cartesian equation for the line $l$ that passes through the point $(1,-2,4)$ and is parallel to the line with equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.answer: The direction is $(5,2,-1)$, so $l:\ x=1+5\mu,\ y=-2+2\mu,\ z=4-\mu$. Eliminating $\mu$: $\dfrac{x-1}5=\dfrac{y+2}2=4-z$.

questions.question: The line $l$ has Cartesian equation $\dfrac{x-1}5=\dfrac{y+2}2=4-z$. Determine where $l$ meets the $xz$-plane.
questions.answer: The $xz$-plane is $y=0$: $\dfrac{0+2}2=1$, so $x-1=5$ giving $x=6$, and $4-z=1$ giving $z=3$. It meets the $xz$-plane at $(6,0,3)$.

prev.question: Find the Cartesian equation for the line $l$ that passes through the point $(1,-2,4)$ and is parallel to the line with equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
prev.answer: The direction is $(5,2,-1)$, so $l:\ x=1+5\mu,\ y=-2+2\mu,\ z=4-\mu$. Eliminating $\mu$: $\dfrac{x-1}5=\dfrac{y+2}2=4-z$.

questions.question: Prove that $\log_29$ is irrational.
questions.answer: Assume $\log_29=\dfrac ab$ is rational, where $a,b$ are positive integers (it is positive as $9>1$). Then $2^{a/b}=9$, so $2^a=9^b$. The left side is even and the right side is odd (for positive integers $a,b$). This is a contradiction, so $\log_29$ is irrational.

questions.question: If $\omega$ is a complex solution of $z^3=1$, simplify $(1+\omega)^2+(1+\omega^2)^2$.
questions.answer: $\omega\ne1$ satisfies $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$, so $1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $1+\omega^2=-\omega$. Then $(1+\omega)^2+(1+\omega^2)^2=\omega^4+\omega^2=\omega+\omega^2=-1$.

questions.question: Write the negation of the statement $\exists x\in\mathbb R^+,\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^+:\ xy=1$.
questions.answer: $\forall x\in\mathbb R^+,\ \exists y\in\mathbb R^+:\ xy\ne1$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\log_e(x^2+1)\,dx$.
questions.answer: By parts with $u=\ln(x^2+1)$, $dv=dx$: $\displaystyle\int_0^1\ln(x^2+1)dx=\Big[x\ln(x^2+1)\Big]_0^1-\int_0^1\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+1}dx=\ln2-\int_0^1\left(2-\dfrac2{x^2+1}\right)dx=\ln2-\Big[2x-2\tan^{-1}x\Big]_0^1=\ln2-2+\dfrac\pi2$.

questions.question: Consider the spheres $S_1:\ x^2-2x+y^2+4y+z^2-4z=0$ and $S_2:\ x^2+y^2+z^2+10x+2z+10=0$. Explain why $S_1$ and $S_2$ intersect at a single point. (Do NOT find this point.)
questions.answer: Completing the square, $S_1:\ (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2+(z-2)^2=9$, with centre $(1,-2,2)$ and radius 3. $S_2:\ (x+5)^2+y^2+(z+1)^2=16$, with centre $(-5,0,-1)$ and radius 4. The distance between the centres is $\sqrt{6^2+2^2+3^2}=7=3+4$, the sum of the radii, so the spheres touch externally at exactly one point.

questions.question: Consider $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Show that $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.
questions.answer: By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $\dfrac1{z^n}=z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$. Subtracting, $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.

questions.question: Let $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ and use $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$. Hence, or otherwise, find the constants $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $\sin^5\theta=a\sin5\theta+b\sin3\theta+c\sin\theta$.
questions.answer: $\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)^5=(2i\sin\theta)^5=32i\sin^5\theta$. Expanding the left side: $\left(z^5-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)-5\left(z^3-\dfrac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)=2i\sin5\theta-10i\sin3\theta+20i\sin\theta$. So $32i\sin^5\theta=2i(\sin5\theta-5\sin3\theta+10\sin\theta)$ and $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$. Thus $a=\dfrac1{16}$, $b=-\dfrac5{16}$, $c=\dfrac58$.

prev.question: Consider $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Show that $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.
prev.answer: By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $\dfrac1{z^n}=z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$. Subtracting, $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.

questions.question: Given $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}16\sin^5\theta\,d\theta$.
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin5\theta-5\sin3\theta+10\sin\theta)d\theta=\Big[-\dfrac{\cos5\theta}5+\dfrac{5\cos3\theta}3-10\cos\theta\Big]_0^{\pi/2}=0-\left(-\dfrac15+\dfrac53-10\right)=\dfrac{128}{15}$.

prev.answer: By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $\dfrac1{z^n}=z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$. Subtracting, $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.

Expanding the left side: $\left(z^5-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)-5\left(z^3-\dfrac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)=2i\sin5\theta-10i\sin3\theta+20i\sin\theta$. So $32i\sin^5\theta=2i(\sin5\theta-5\sin3\theta+10\sin\theta)$ and $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$. Thus $a=\dfrac1{16}$, $b=-\dfrac5{16}$, $c=\dfrac58$.

questions.question: A cube has a pair of opposite vertices $A(-1,-1,-1)$ and $B(1,1,1)$. Another pair of opposite vertices are $X$ and $Y$, as displayed in the diagram. If $\alpha$ is the acute angle between $AB$ and $XY$, show that $\sin2\alpha=\dfrac{2\sqrt8}{9}$.
questions.answer: With $X(1,-1,-1)$ and $Y(-1,1,1)$ (the diagram's labels), $\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,2,2)$ and $\overrightarrow{XY}=(-2,2,2)$, both of length $2\sqrt3$. $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{|{-4}+4+4|}{12}=\dfrac13$, so $\sin\alpha=\sqrt{1-\dfrac19}=\dfrac{\sqrt8}3$. $\sin2\alpha=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt8}3\cdot\dfrac13=\dfrac{2\sqrt8}9$.

questions.question: Three positive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy $a\ge b\ge c$ and $a+b+c\le1$. By considering $(a+b+c)^2$ or otherwise, prove that $a^2+3b^2+5c^2\le1$.
questions.answer: Since $0<a+b+c\le1$, $(a+b+c)^2\le1$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2+2ab+2bc+2ac\le1$. As $a\ge b\ge c>0$: $2ab\ge2b^2$, $2ac\ge2c^2$ and $2bc\ge2c^2$. Therefore $a^2+b^2+c^2+2b^2+2c^2+2c^2\le a^2+b^2+c^2+2ab+2bc+2ac\le1$, i.e. $a^2+3b^2+5c^2\le1$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u=\sin x-x\cos x$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\dfrac{x}{1-x\cot x}dx$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{du}{dx}=\cos x-\cos x+x\sin x=x\sin x$. $\dfrac x{1-x\cot x}=\dfrac{x\sin x}{\sin x-x\cos x}$, so the integral is $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{du}u$. At $x=\dfrac\pi2$, $u=1$; at $x=\pi$, $u=\pi$. The value is $\ln\pi-\ln1=\ln\pi$.

questions.question: Consider the four expressions, where $a>0$ and $b>0$: $D=\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$, $U=\sqrt{ab}$, $B=\dfrac{a+b}2$, $O=\sqrt{\dfrac{a^2+b^2}2}$. Show that $D\le U\le B\le O$.
questions.answer:
$B\ge U$: $(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\ge0\Rightarrow a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$, so $\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}$.

$U\ge D$: from $a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$, $\dfrac{2\sqrt{ab}}{a+b}\le1$. Multiplying both sides by $\sqrt{ab}>0$ gives $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}\le\sqrt{ab}$, i.e. $D\le U$.

$B\le O$: both are positive so compare squares. $\left(\dfrac{a+b}2\right)^2\le\dfrac{a^2+b^2}2\iff a^2+2ab+b^2\le2a^2+2b^2\iff0\le(a-b)^2$, which is true.

Hence $D\le U\le B\le O$.

questions.question: The triangle $ABC$ in the complex plane is formed from the points $A(\alpha)$, $B(\beta)$ and $C(\gamma)$. The complex numbers $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ satisfy $\dfrac{\gamma-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha}=1-i$ and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$. Calculate $\alpha:\beta$.
questions.answer: $\gamma=-\alpha-\beta$, so $\dfrac{-2\alpha-\beta}{\beta-\alpha}=1-i$. Then $-2\alpha-\beta=(1-i)(\beta-\alpha)=\beta-i\beta-\alpha+i\alpha$, so $-\alpha(1+i)=\beta(2-i)$ and $\dfrac\alpha\beta=\dfrac{-2+i}{1+i}=\dfrac{(-2+i)(1-i)}{2}=\dfrac{-1+3i}2$. So $\alpha:\beta=(-1+3i):2$. (In terms of lengths, $|\alpha|:|\beta|=\sqrt{10}:2$.)

questions.question: Two magpies, $A$ and $B$, are observed flying. Their initial positions are $(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$ m and $(-2\mathbf i+a\mathbf j+6\mathbf k)$ m, where $a$ is a constant. They are travelling with constant velocities $(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+6\mathbf k)$ m/s and $(3\mathbf i+12\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$ m/s respectively. Determine the constant $a$, if the distance between the two magpies is least after 5 seconds.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}(t)=(-2+3t-1-2t,\ a+12t+2-3t,\ 6+4t-4-6t)=(t-3,\ 9t+a+2,\ 2-2t)$. $D^2=(t-3)^2+(9t+a+2)^2+(2-2t)^2$, a quadratic in $t$ with positive leading coefficient, so its minimum is where $\dfrac{d(D^2)}{dt}=0$: $2(t-3)+18(9t+a+2)-4(2-2t)=0$. At $t=5$: $4+18(a+47)+32=0$, so $a+47=-2$ and $a=-49$.

questions.question: By considering $(1+i)(4-i)^2$ prove that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac7{23}+2\tan^{-1}\dfrac14=\dfrac\pi4$.
questions.answer: $(4-i)^2=15-8i$, so $(1+i)(4-i)^2=15-8i+15i+8=23+7i$. Arguments: $\arg(1+i)=\dfrac\pi4$, $\arg(4-i)=-\tan^{-1}\dfrac14$ and $\arg(23+7i)=\tan^{-1}\dfrac7{23}$ (first quadrant). Since $\dfrac\pi4-2\tan^{-1}\dfrac14\in(-\pi,\pi]$ equals the principal argument of the product, $\dfrac\pi4-2\tan^{-1}\dfrac14=\tan^{-1}\dfrac7{23}$. Rearranging, $\tan^{-1}\dfrac7{23}+2\tan^{-1}\dfrac14=\dfrac\pi4$.

questions.question:
A body of unit mass falls vertically from rest, under gravity, from a height of 100 metres above the ground through a resisting medium. The resistance to its motion is $\dfrac{v^2}{100}$, where $v$ is the speed of the body (in m/s) after falling a distance $x$ metres.

Show that the acceleration $\ddot x$ of the body is given by $\ddot x=g-\dfrac{v^2}{100}$.
questions.answer: Taking downward as positive, the forces on the unit mass are gravity $g$ down and resistance $\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ up. By Newton's second law $\ddot x=g-\dfrac{v^2}{100}$.

questions.question:
A body of unit mass falls vertically from rest, under gravity, from a height of 100 metres above the ground through a resisting medium. The resistance to its motion is $\dfrac{v^2}{100}$, where $v$ is the speed of the body (in m/s) after falling a distance $x$ metres. The acceleration is $\ddot x=g-\dfrac{v^2}{100}$.

Determine the terminal velocity $V$ of the body.
questions.answer: At terminal velocity $\ddot x=0$: $g-\dfrac{V^2}{100}=0$, so $V^2=100g$ and $V=10\sqrt g$ m/s.

questions.question:
A body of unit mass falls vertically from rest, under gravity, from a height of 100 metres above the ground through a resisting medium. The resistance to its motion is $\dfrac{v^2}{100}$, where $v$ is the speed of the body (in m/s) after falling a distance $x$ metres. The acceleration is $\ddot x=g-\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ and the terminal velocity is $V=10\sqrt g$.

Show that the velocity $v$ of the body after it has fallen a vertical distance $x$ is given by $v^2=V^2\left(1-e^{-x/50}\right)$.
questions.answer: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=g-\dfrac{v^2}{100}=\dfrac{V^2-v^2}{100}$ (since $V^2=100g$). Separating, $\dfrac{v\,dv}{V^2-v^2}=\dfrac{dx}{100}$, so $-\dfrac12\ln(V^2-v^2)=\dfrac x{100}+C$, i.e. $\ln(V^2-v^2)=-\dfrac x{50}+C'$. At $x=0$, $v=0$: $C'=\ln V^2$. Hence $V^2-v^2=V^2e^{-x/50}$ and $v^2=V^2\left(1-e^{-x/50}\right)$.

Determine the distance fallen when the velocity of the body first reaches $\dfrac V2$.
questions.answer: $\left(\dfrac V2\right)^2=V^2\left(1-e^{-x/50}\right)\Rightarrow\dfrac14=1-e^{-x/50}\Rightarrow e^{-x/50}=\dfrac34\Rightarrow x=50\ln\dfrac43\approx14.4$ m.

questions.question: Let $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{p=1}^n\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac1{2p^2}\right)$. Prove by induction that $\tan(S_n)=\dfrac n{n+1}$.
questions.answer:
Base case $n=1$: $S_1=\tan^{-1}\dfrac12$ so $\tan S_1=\dfrac12=\dfrac1{1+1}$. True.

Assume $\tan S_k=\dfrac k{k+1}$. Then $S_{k+1}=S_k+\tan^{-1}\dfrac1{2(k+1)^2}$ and
$\tan S_{k+1}=\dfrac{\frac k{k+1}+\frac1{2(k+1)^2}}{1-\frac k{k+1}\cdot\frac1{2(k+1)^2}}=\dfrac{(2k^2+2k+1)/(2(k+1)^2)}{(2(k+1)^3-k)/(2(k+1)^3)}=\dfrac{(k+1)(2k^2+2k+1)}{2k^3+6k^2+5k+2}$.
Since $2k^3+6k^2+5k+2=(k+2)(2k^2+2k+1)$, $\tan S_{k+1}=\dfrac{k+1}{k+2}$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$.

By induction it is true for all integers $n\ge1$.

questions.question: The solutions of $z^5=1$ can be joined to form a regular pentagon in the complex plane, as shown. For $n\ge3$, show that the perimeter of the regular $n$-gon formed by the solutions of $z^n=1$ is $P_n=2n\sin\left(\dfrac\pi n\right)$.
questions.answer: The solutions of $z^n=1$ lie on the unit circle, with consecutive roots separated by $\dfrac{2\pi}n$ at the origin. Each side is the base of an isosceles triangle with two sides of length 1 and apex angle $\dfrac{2\pi}n$. By the cosine rule, the side length $s$ satisfies $s^2=1+1-2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}n=2\left(1-\cos\dfrac{2\pi}n\right)=4\sin^2\dfrac\pi n$, so $s=2\sin\dfrac\pi n$. With $n$ sides, $P_n=2n\sin\dfrac\pi n$.

questions.question: The perimeter of the regular $n$-gon formed by the solutions of $z^n=1$ is $P_n=2n\sin\left(\dfrac\pi n\right)$. It is known that as $x\to0$, $\dfrac{\sin x}x\to1$ (do not prove this). Using this, show that as $n\to\infty$, $P_n\to2\pi$.
questions.answer: Write $P_n=2\pi\cdot\dfrac{\sin(\pi/n)}{\pi/n}$. As $n\to\infty$, $x=\dfrac\pi n\to0$, so $\dfrac{\sin x}x\to1$. Hence $P_n\to2\pi\times1=2\pi$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{1/4}\dfrac{x^n}{e^x}dx$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$. Calculate $I_1$.
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{1/4}\dfrac{x^n}{e^x}dx$. Show that $kI_k=I_{k+1}-I_k+\dfrac{\left(\frac14\right)^{k+1}}{e^{1/4}}$.
questions.answer: By parts with $u=x^{k+1}$, $dv=e^{-x}dx$: $I_{k+1}=\Big[-x^{k+1}e^{-x}\Big]_0^{1/4}+(k+1)\displaystyle\int_0^{1/4}x^ke^{-x}dx=-\dfrac{(1/4)^{k+1}}{e^{1/4}}+(k+1)I_k$. Rearranging, $kI_k=I_{k+1}-I_k+\dfrac{(1/4)^{k+1}}{e^{1/4}}$.

prev.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{1/4}\dfrac{x^n}{e^x}dx$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$. Calculate $I_1$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{1/4}\dfrac{x^n}{e^x}dx$ and use $kI_k=I_{k+1}-I_k+\dfrac{(1/4)^{k+1}}{e^{1/4}}$. Deduce that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nkI_k=I_{n+1}-I_1+\dfrac{1-\left(\frac14\right)^n}{12e^{1/4}}$.
questions.answer: Summing the identity for $k=1$ to $n$: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nkI_k=\sum_{k=1}^n(I_{k+1}-I_k)+\dfrac1{e^{1/4}}\sum_{k=1}^n\left(\dfrac14\right)^{k+1}$. The first sum telescopes to $I_{n+1}-I_1$. The second is a geometric series with first term $\dfrac1{16}$ and ratio $\dfrac14$: $\dfrac{\frac1{16}\left(1-\left(\frac14\right)^n\right)}{1-\frac14}=\dfrac{1-\left(\frac14\right)^n}{12}$. Hence $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nkI_k=I_{n+1}-I_1+\dfrac{1-\left(\frac14\right)^n}{12e^{1/4}}$.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a regular tetrahedron $OABC$ with sides of length 1. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the edges such that $BX:XC=AY:YB=x:1-x$, where $0<x<1$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$.

Show that $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac12$.
questions.answer: Each face is an equilateral triangle, so the angle between any two edges from $O$ is $\dfrac\pi3$. With all edges of length 1, $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac12$, and similarly $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac12$.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a regular tetrahedron $OABC$ with sides of length 1. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the edges such that $BX:XC=AY:YB=x:1-x$, where $0<x<1$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. You may use $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac12$.

Show that $|\overrightarrow{OY}|=\sqrt{1-x+x^2}$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OY}=\overrightarrow{OA}+x\overrightarrow{AB}=(1-x)\mathbf a+x\mathbf b$. $|\overrightarrow{OY}|^2=(1-x)^2|\mathbf a|^2+2x(1-x)\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+x^2|\mathbf b|^2=(1-x)^2+x(1-x)+x^2=1-x+x^2$. So $|\overrightarrow{OY}|=\sqrt{1-x+x^2}$.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a regular tetrahedron $OABC$ with sides of length 1. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the edges such that $BX:XC=AY:YB=x:1-x$, where $0<x<1$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. You may use $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=\dfrac12$ and $|\overrightarrow{OY}|=\sqrt{1-x+x^2}$.

Determine the range of values of $\angle YOX$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{OY}=(1-x)\mathbf a+x\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OX}=\overrightarrow{OB}+x\overrightarrow{BC}=(1-x)\mathbf b+x\mathbf c$, which also has length $\sqrt{1-x+x^2}$.

$\overrightarrow{OY}\cdot\overrightarrow{OX}=\tfrac12(1-x)^2+\tfrac12x(1-x)+x(1-x)+\tfrac12x^2=\dfrac{1+x-x^2}2$.

Hence $\cos\angle YOX=\dfrac{1+x-x^2}{2(1-x+x^2)}$.

At $x\to0$ or $x\to1$, $\cos\angle YOX\to\dfrac12$. Differentiating, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos\angle YOX=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2-4x}{(1-x+x^2)^2}$, which is zero at $x=\dfrac12$, positive for $x<\dfrac12$ and negative for $x>\dfrac12$, so $x=\dfrac12$ is a maximum: $\cos\angle YOX=\dfrac{1+\frac12-\frac14}{2\left(\frac34\right)}=\dfrac56$.

So $\dfrac12<\cos\angle YOX\le\dfrac56$, and since cosine is decreasing on $\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$, $\cos^{-1}\dfrac56\le\angle YOX<\dfrac\pi3$.

questions.question: Given $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$, what is the magnitude of the vector $(\cos\theta)\mathbf i+(\sin\theta)\mathbf j+(\tan\theta)\mathbf k$?
questions.answer: $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta+\tan^2\theta}=\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}=\sqrt{\sec^2\theta}=\sec\theta$, since $\sec\theta>0$ in the first quadrant (D).

questions.question: Which is the negation of the following statement? "If snow is falling, then I will not be at the park."
questions.answer: $\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q$. Here $Q$ is \"I will not be at the park\", so the negation is \"Snow is falling and I will be at the park\" (C).
options: If snow is falling, then I will be at the park.
If snow is not falling, then I will be at the park.
Snow is falling and I will be at the park.
Snow is not falling and I will be at the park.

questions.question: A particle whose displacement is $x$ moves in simple harmonic motion such that $\ddot x=-4x$. What is $x$ as a function of $t$ if initially $x=3$ and $\dot x=-6\sqrt3$?
questions.answer: $n=2$ and the centre is $x=0$. Try $x=3\cos2t-3\sqrt3\sin2t$: $x(0)=3$ and $\dot x=-6\sin2t-6\sqrt3\cos2t$, so $\dot x(0)=-6\sqrt3$. Both conditions hold (A).

questions.question: The complex number $z$ is shown on the Argand diagram. Which of the following best represents $i\bar z$? (Diagrams A–D are shown below the Argand diagram, in order.)
questions.answer: $z$ is in the first quadrant at an angle of about $20^\circ$. $\bar z$ is at $-20^\circ$ with the same modulus, and multiplying by $i$ rotates it by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise to about $70^\circ$, still on the unit circle. This is diagram A.

questions.question: $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are three collinear points with position vectors $\mathbf p$, $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf r$ respectively. $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$ such that $PQ:QR=2:1$. The position vector of $R$ is given by:
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PR}=\dfrac32\overrightarrow{PQ}$, so $\mathbf r=\mathbf p+\dfrac32(\mathbf q-\mathbf p)=-\dfrac12\mathbf p+\dfrac32\mathbf q$ (C).

questions.question: For which of these statements, for positive integers $x$ and $y$, is the converse necessarily true?
questions.answer: A: $4+6$ is even but 4 and 6 are not odd, so the converse is false. B: $2^2+4^2$ is even, so the converse is false. C: if $xy$ is odd then neither $x$ nor $y$ can be even, so both are odd: the converse is true. D: $3^4$ is odd but $y=4$ is even, so the converse is false (C).
options: If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x+y$ is even.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x^2+y^2$ is even.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $xy$ is odd.
If $x$ and $y$ are odd, then $x^y$ is odd.

questions.question: Which of the following lines passes through $(0,1,-1)$?
questions.answer: A and C have $x=1$ throughout, so they cannot reach $x=0$. B: $\lambda=-1$ gives $(1-1,\,1-0,\,0-1)=(0,1,-1)$. D: $\lambda=-1$ gives $(0,-1,1)$, which is not the point (B).

questions.question: Which of these inequalities is false?
questions.answer: A: $\dfrac1{1+x}<\dfrac1x$ on $[1,2]$. B: $\sin x<1$. C: $e^{-x^2}$ is decreasing, so its values on $[1,2]$ are below those on $[0,1]$. D: on $[0,\pi/4]$, $0\le\tan x\le1$ so $\tan^2x\ge\tan^3x$ and the inequality is reversed, so it is false (D).

questions.question: Which parametric form best describes the curve below?
questions.answer: All options have a unit-circle projection in the $xy$-plane. The curve spirals down towards the plane $z=0$ while circling, so $z$ decays towards 0, not linearly (A), not like $\ln t$ (C, which would be large negative near $t=0$) and not oscillating (D). Only $z=e^{-0.5t}$ decays towards 0 (B).
options: $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(t)\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(e^{-0.5t})\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(\ln t)\mathbf k$
$\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t)\mathbf i+(\sin t)\mathbf j+(\cos2t)\mathbf k$

questions.question: Let $\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi i}5}$. What is the value of $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)(1-\omega^3)(1-\omega^4)$?
questions.answer: $\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3,\omega^4$ are the non-real roots of $z^5=1$, so $z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1=(z-\omega)(z-\omega^2)(z-\omega^3)(z-\omega^4)$. Putting $z=1$: $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)(1-\omega^3)(1-\omega^4)=1+1+1+1+1=5$ (D).

questions.question: Use integration by parts to find $\displaystyle\int\ln(x^2+1)\,dx$.
questions.answer: $u=\ln(x^2+1)$, $dv=dx$, $du=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}dx$, $v=x$. $\displaystyle\int\ln(x^2+1)dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-\int\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+1}dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-2\int\left(1-\dfrac1{x^2+1}\right)dx=x\ln(x^2+1)-2x+2\tan^{-1}x+C$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $u=e^x-1$ to find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{e^{2x}}{(e^x-1)^2}dx$.
questions.answer: $e^x=u+1$ and $du=e^xdx=(u+1)dx$. $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{(u+1)^2}{u^2}\cdot\dfrac1{u+1}du=\int\dfrac{u+1}{u^2}du=\int\left(\dfrac1u+\dfrac1{u^2}\right)du=\ln|u|-\dfrac1u+C=\ln|e^x-1|-\dfrac1{e^x-1}+C$.

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac1{3\cos x-4\sin x+5}dx$.
questions.answer: $\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, $\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$; $x=0\to t=0$ and $x=\dfrac\pi2\to t=1$. The denominator is $\dfrac{3(1-t^2)-8t+5(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}=\dfrac{2t^2-8t+8}{1+t^2}=\dfrac{2(t-2)^2}{1+t^2}$. So $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{1+t^2}{2(t-2)^2}\cdot\dfrac2{1+t^2}dt=\int_0^1(t-2)^{-2}dt=\Big[-\dfrac1{t-2}\Big]_0^1=1-\dfrac12=\dfrac12$.

questions.question: Convert the line $y=3x-5$ to the form $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b$.
questions.answer: The gradient 3 gives a direction vector $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, and $(0,-5)$ lies on the line: $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: It is known that $5+6i$ is a zero of the polynomial $P(z)=2z^3-19z^2+112z+k$, where $k$ is real. Find the other two zeroes of $P(z)$.
questions.answer: The coefficients are real, so $5-6i$ is also a zero. Sum of zeroes $=\dfrac{19}2$: $(5+6i)+(5-6i)+\alpha=\dfrac{19}2$, so $\alpha=-\dfrac12$. The other zeroes are $5-6i$ and $-\dfrac12$.

questions.question: It is known that $5+6i$ and $5-6i$ and $-\dfrac12$ are the zeroes of $P(z)=2z^3-19z^2+112z+k$, where $k$ is real. Find the value of $k$.
questions.answer: Product of zeroes $=-\dfrac k2$: $(5+6i)(5-6i)\left(-\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{61}2=-\dfrac k2$, so $k=61$.

questions.question: Prove that $\sqrt[3]2$ is irrational.
questions.answer: Assume $\sqrt[3]2=\dfrac pq$ with $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ and $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Then $2q^3=p^3$, so $p^3$ is even, hence $p$ is even (contrapositive: odd$^3$ is odd). Let $p=2m$: $2q^3=8m^3$, so $q^3=4m^3$ is even and $q$ is even. But then $p$ and $q$ share the factor 2, contradicting $\gcd(p,q)=1$. So $\sqrt[3]2$ is irrational.

questions.question: Given that $x$ is a real number and $(x+i)^4$ is purely imaginary, find all possible values of $x$ in exact form.
questions.answer: $(x+i)^4=x^4+4x^3i-6x^2-4xi+1=(x^4-6x^2+1)+(4x^3-4x)i$. The real part must be zero: $x^4-6x^2+1=0$, so $x^2=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{32}}2=3\pm2\sqrt2=(\sqrt2\pm1)^2$. Hence $x=\pm(\sqrt2+1)$ or $x=\pm(\sqrt2-1)$. (For these, $4x(x^2-1)\ne0$, so the number is non-zero.)

questions.question: Find all the solutions of $z^5=4+4i$, giving your answers in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer: $4+4i=4\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$. Let $z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta$: $r^5=4\sqrt2=2^{5/2}$ so $r=\sqrt2$, and $5\theta=\dfrac\pi4+2k\pi$. So $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi{20}+\dfrac{2k\pi}5\right)$, $k=0,1,2,3,4$.

questions.question: On an Argand diagram sketch the locus of the point $P$ representing the complex number $z$ such that $|z-(\sqrt3+i)|=1$.
questions.answer: A circle with centre $(\sqrt3,1)$ and radius 1 (it passes through the origin's neighbourhood: the origin is at distance 2 from the centre, so the circle does not contain the origin).

questions.question: For the locus $|z-(\sqrt3+i)|=1$, find the maximum possible values of $|z|$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$.
questions.answer: The centre $\sqrt3+i$ has modulus 2 and argument $\dfrac\pi6$. Maximum $|z|=2+1=3$. The maximum argument occurs at the tangent from the origin: $\sin\alpha=\dfrac12$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$ and the maximum $\operatorname{Arg}z=\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi3$.

questions.question: Prove that for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, $\dfrac{(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2}2\ge x+y$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2}2-x-y=\dfrac{x^2-2x+1+y^2+4y+4-2x-2y}2=\dfrac{x^2-4x+4+y^2+2y+1}2=\dfrac{(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2}2\ge0$, as the sum of two squares is non-negative. Hence the inequality holds.

questions.question: A particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion centred about the origin. Its equation of motion is $\ddot x=-16x$. Show that $v^2=16(a^2-x^2)$, where $a$ is the amplitude.
questions.answer: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-16x$, so $\dfrac12v^2=-8x^2+C$ and $v^2=-16x^2+C_1$. At the amplitude $x=a$, $v=0$: $C_1=16a^2$. So $v^2=16(a^2-x^2)$.

questions.question: A particle's position at time $t$ seconds is given by $x=\sqrt3\sin4t-\cos4t$. Express $x$ in the form $R\sin(4t-\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is in radians.
questions.answer: $R\sin(4t-\alpha)=R\sin4t\cos\alpha-R\cos4t\sin\alpha$. So $R\cos\alpha=\sqrt3$ and $R\sin\alpha=1$: $R=\sqrt{3+1}=2$ and $\tan\alpha=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$. $x=2\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)$.

questions.question: A particle's position at time $t$ seconds is $x=2\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)$. When does the particle first reach its maximum speed after $t=0$?
questions.answer: Maximum speed occurs at the centre of motion, $x=0$: $\sin\left(4t-\dfrac\pi6\right)=0$, so $4t-\dfrac\pi6=0,\pi,\dots$. The first positive solution is $4t=\dfrac\pi6$, so $t=\dfrac\pi{24}$ seconds.

questions.question: If $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $z-\dfrac1z=2i\sin\theta$ and $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.
questions.answer: $|z|=1$, so $\dfrac1z=\bar z=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$ and $z-\dfrac1z=2i\sin\theta$. By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $\dfrac1{z^n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$, so $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$.

questions.question: Using $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$ with $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$.
questions.answer: $\sin^5\theta=\left(\dfrac1{2i}\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)\right)^5=\dfrac1{32i}\left(z^5-5z^3+10z-\dfrac{10}z+\dfrac5{z^3}-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)=\dfrac1{32i}\left[\left(z^5-\dfrac1{z^5}\right)-5\left(z^3-\dfrac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z-\dfrac1z\right)\right]=\dfrac{2i\sin5\theta-10i\sin3\theta+20i\sin\theta}{32i}=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$.

questions.question:
Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

What type of quadrilateral best describes $OACB$?
questions.answer: $OA=|z|=1$, $OB=|z^2|=1$, and $AC=|z^2|=1$, $BC=|z|=1$ (as $C$ is found by vector addition). All four sides are equal, so $OACB$ is a rhombus.

questions.question:
Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

Find $\arg(z+z^2)$ in terms of $\theta$.
questions.answer: The diagonal $OC$ of a rhombus bisects the angle $AOB=2\theta-\theta=\theta$, so $\arg(z+z^2)=\theta+\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac{3\theta}2$.

Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ where $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. On the Argand diagram the point $A$ represents $z$, the point $B$ represents $z^2$ and the point $C$ represents $z+z^2$.

Find $|z+z^2|$ in terms of $\theta$.
questions.answer: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$; the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. In right triangle $OMA$, $\dfrac{OM}{OA}=\cos\dfrac\theta2$ with $OA=1$, so $OM=\cos\dfrac\theta2$ and $|z+z^2|=OC=2\cos\dfrac\theta2$.

questions.question: Prove that $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ for positive real numbers $x,y$.
questions.answer: $(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\ge0$, so $x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0$, i.e. $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$.

questions.question: Using $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ for positive $x,y$, prove that for positive real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$: $a^2+4b^2+4c^2+d^2\ge8\sqrt{abcd}$.
questions.answer: By the result, $a^2+4b^2\ge2\sqrt{4a^2b^2}=4ab$ and $4c^2+d^2\ge2\sqrt{4c^2d^2}=4cd$. Adding, $a^2+4b^2+4c^2+d^2\ge4ab+4cd\ge2\sqrt{16abcd}=8\sqrt{abcd}$.

prev.question: Prove that $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$ for positive real numbers $x,y$.
prev.answer: $(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)^2\ge0$, so $x-2\sqrt{xy}+y\ge0$, i.e. $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$.

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $A$ be the point corresponding to $\lambda=1$ and let $P(6,0,2)$ be a point not on the line. Find the projection of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ onto the line.
questions.answer: $A=(-3,-1,0)$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}=(9,1,2)$. The direction is $\mathbf d=(2,-2,1)$ with $|\mathbf d|^2=9$. $\text{proj}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf d}\mathbf d=\dfrac{18-2+2}9\mathbf d=2\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $A$ be the point corresponding to $\lambda=1$ and let $P(6,0,2)$ be a point not on the line. The projection of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ onto the line is $\overrightarrow{AX}=(4,-4,2)$, where $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$. Hence find the coordinates of the point $P'$, the reflection of $P$ about the line.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{PX}=\overrightarrow{AX}-\overrightarrow{AP}=(4,-4,2)-(9,1,2)=(-5,-5,0)$. $P'$ is the reflection of $P$ in the line, so $\overrightarrow{PP'}=2\overrightarrow{PX}=(-10,-10,0)$ and $\overrightarrow{OP'}=(6,0,2)+(-10,-10,0)=(-4,-10,2)$. So $P'=(-4,-10,2)$.

questions.question: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$.
questions.answer: $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos^3\theta+3i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-i\sin^3\theta$. By de Moivre the left side is $\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta$. Equating real parts, $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$; equating imaginary parts, $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$.

questions.question: Using $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$, deduce that $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$.
questions.answer: $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta}{\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta}$. Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\cos^3\theta$ gives $\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$, which equals $\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}$ (multiply top and bottom by $-1$).

prev.question: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$.

questions.question: Given $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}$, by letting $x=\tan\theta$, find the solutions of $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0$, expressing them in exact trigonometric form.
questions.answer: Put $x=\tan\theta$: $\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta=3\tan^2\theta-1$, so $\dfrac{\tan^3\theta-3\tan\theta}{3\tan^2\theta-1}=1$, i.e. $\tan3\theta=1$. Then $3\theta=\dfrac\pi4+k\pi$, so $\theta=\dfrac\pi{12},\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{9\pi}{12}$. The solutions are $x=\tan\dfrac\pi{12},\ \tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \tan\dfrac{3\pi}4=-1$.

questions.question: The solutions of $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0$ are $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}$, $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ and $-1$. Hence show that $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=4$.
questions.answer: The sum of the roots is $-\dfrac{-3}{1}=3$: $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}-1=3$, so $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=4$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^2\sqrt{8-2x-x^2}\,dx$ using a suitable substitution.
questions.answer: $8-2x-x^2=9-(x+1)^2$. Let $x+1=3\sin\theta$, $dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$; $x=-1\to\theta=0$ and $x=2\to\theta=\dfrac\pi2$. $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{9-9\sin^2\theta}\,3\cos\theta\,d\theta=9\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac92\int_0^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)d\theta=\dfrac92\left[\theta+\dfrac12\sin2\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\dfrac{9\pi}4$. (This is a quarter of a circle of radius 3.)

questions.question: Prove the following statement for all integers $n\ge3$: \"If $3^n-4$ is a prime, then $n$ is odd.\"
questions.answer: The contrapositive is: if $n$ is even, then $3^n-4$ is not prime. Let $n=2m$, $m\ge2$. Then $3^{2m}-4=(3^m)^2-2^2=(3^m-2)(3^m+2)$. Since $m\ge2$, $3^m-2\ge7>1$ and $3^m+2>1$, so $3^n-4$ has factors other than 1 and itself and is not prime. The contrapositive is true, so the statement is true.

questions.question:
A particle of mass $m$ kilograms is dropped from rest in a medium where the resistance to motion has magnitude $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ newtons when the velocity of the particle is $v$ m/s. After $t$ seconds, the particle has fallen $x$ metres. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$.

With a diagram, show that the acceleration is $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$.
questions.answer: Taking downwards as positive, the forces are $mg$ down and the resistance $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ up (a diagram shows these two arrows on the particle). $m\ddot x=mg-\dfrac1{10}mv^2=10m-\dfrac1{10}mv^2$, so $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ kilograms is dropped from rest in a medium where the resistance to motion has magnitude $\dfrac1{10}mv^2$ newtons when the velocity of the particle is $v$ m/s. After $t$ seconds, the particle has fallen $x$ metres. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$. The acceleration is $\ddot x=\dfrac1{10}(100-v^2)$. The particle hits the ground $\log_e\left(\sqrt5\right)$ seconds after it is dropped. Find its distance fallen in simplest exact form.
questions.answer:
Velocity at the time: $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{100-v^2}{10}$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dv}{100-v^2}=\int\dfrac{dt}{10}$. Since $\dfrac1{100-v^2}=\dfrac1{20}\left(\dfrac1{10-v}+\dfrac1{10+v}\right)$, $\dfrac1{20}\ln\left|\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}\right|=\dfrac t{10}+C$. With $v=0$ at $t=0$, $C=0$, so $\ln\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}=2t$ (for $0\le v<10$). At $t=\ln\sqrt5$: $\ln\dfrac{10+v}{10-v}=\ln5$, so $10+v=50-5v$ and $v=\dfrac{20}3$ m/s.

Distance: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{100-v^2}{10}$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{v\,dv}{100-v^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{10}$, giving $-\dfrac12\ln(100-v^2)=\dfrac x{10}+C$. At $x=0$, $v=0$: $C=-\dfrac12\ln100$. So $x=-5\ln\dfrac{100-v^2}{100}$. At $v=\dfrac{20}3$: $\dfrac{100-\frac{400}9}{100}=\dfrac59$, so $x=-5\ln\dfrac59=5\ln\dfrac95$ metres.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x^n}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$ for integers $n\ge0$. Show that $I_n=\dfrac{\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}}{n}$ for all integers $n\ge2$.
questions.answer: Write $I_n=\int_0^1x^{n-1}\cdot\dfrac x{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$ and integrate by parts with $u=x^{n-1}$, $dv=\dfrac x{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx$, so $du=(n-1)x^{n-2}dx$ and $v=\sqrt{1+x^2}$. $I_n=\Big[x^{n-1}\sqrt{1+x^2}\Big]_0^1-(n-1)\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{n-2}\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=\sqrt2-(n-1)\int_0^1\dfrac{x^{n-2}(1+x^2)}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dx=\sqrt2-(n-1)(I_{n-2}+I_n)$. So $nI_n=\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}$ and $I_n=\dfrac{\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}}n$.

questions.question: The diagram shows a rectangular prism in the first octant created from $P(p,q,r)$ with all edges parallel to the axes and with $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$ as face diagonals ($A(p,q,0)$, $B(p,0,r)$, $C(0,q,r)$). It is known that $\angle AOB=\angle AOC=\angle BOC=\dfrac\pi3$. Prove that the rectangular prism is a cube.
questions.answer:
$\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}}{|OA||OB|}$, so $\dfrac12=\dfrac{p^2}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\sqrt{p^2+r^2}}$ (1). Similarly $\dfrac12=\dfrac{q^2}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\sqrt{q^2+r^2}}$ (2) and $\dfrac12=\dfrac{r^2}{\sqrt{p^2+r^2}\sqrt{q^2+r^2}}$ (3).

(1)=(2): $p^2\sqrt{q^2+r^2}=q^2\sqrt{p^2+r^2}$. Squaring, $p^4(q^2+r^2)=q^4(p^2+r^2)$, so $p^2q^2(p^2-q^2)+r^2(p^2-q^2)(p^2+q^2)=0$, i.e. $(p^2-q^2)\left[p^2q^2+r^2(p^2+q^2)\right]=0$. The bracket is positive since $p,q,r>0$, so $p^2=q^2$ and $p=q$. Similarly (1)=(3) gives $p=r$. Hence $p=q=r$ and the prism is a cube.

questions.question: Show that for $k\ge0$, $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$.
questions.answer: Both sides are positive, so compare squares. $(2k+3)^2=4k^2+12k+9$ and $4(k+1)(k+2)=4k^2+12k+8$. Since $4k^2+12k+9>4k^2+12k+8$, $(2k+3)^2>4(k+1)(k+2)$, so $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$.

questions.question: Using $2k+3>2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}$ for $k\ge0$, show that for $n\ge1$, $1+\dfrac1{\sqrt2}+\dfrac1{\sqrt3}+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt n}>2\left(\sqrt{n+1}-1\right)$.
questions.answer:
Base case $n=1$: LHS $=1$ and RHS $=2(\sqrt2-1)\approx0.83$, so LHS $>$ RHS.

Assume $1+\dfrac1{\sqrt2}+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt k}>2(\sqrt{k+1}-1)$. Then
$1+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt k}+\dfrac1{\sqrt{k+1}}>2\sqrt{k+1}-2+\dfrac1{\sqrt{k+1}}=\dfrac{2(k+1)+1}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2=\dfrac{2k+3}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2>\dfrac{2\sqrt{(k+1)(k+2)}}{\sqrt{k+1}}-2=2\sqrt{k+2}-2=2(\sqrt{k+2}-1)$
(using part (i)). This is the statement for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all $n\ge1$.
