questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-1}2}dx$, where $n=1,2,3,\dots$ Show that $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ for $n=2,3,4,\dots$
questions.answer:
Integrate by parts with $u=\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-1}2}$, $dv=dx$, so $du=\frac{n-1}2\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-3}2}(-2x)\,dx$ and $v=x$:
$$I_n=\left[x\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-1}2}\right]_0^1+(n-1)\int_0^1x^2\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-3}2}dx.$$
The bracket is $0$ (for $n\ge2$). Write $x^2=1-\left(1-x^2\right)$:
$$I_n=(n-1)\int_0^1\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-3}2}dx-(n-1)\int_0^1\left(1-x^2\right)^{\frac{n-1}2}dx=(n-1)I_{n-2}-(n-1)I_n.$$
So $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a straight line under the action of a force $F$ where $F=\dfrac m{x^3}(6-10x)$ and $x$ is its displacement from the origin. Find its velocity if the particle starts from rest at $x=1$.
questions.answer:
$m\ddot x=F\Rightarrow v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{6-10x}{x^3}=6x^{-3}-10x^{-2}$.
$$\tfrac12v^2=-3x^{-2}+10x^{-1}+C.$$
At $x=1$, $v=0$: $0=-3+10+C$, so $C=-7$. Then
$$v^2=-\frac6{x^2}+\frac{20}x-14=\frac{20x-14x^2-6}{x^2}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\pm\frac{\sqrt{20x-14x^2-6}}x.$$
At $x=1$, $\ddot x=6-10=-4<0$, so the particle starts moving in the negative direction: $v=-\dfrac{\sqrt{20x-14x^2-6}}x$.

questions.question: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v$ given by $v^2=\dfrac{20x-14x^2-6}{x^2}$, starting from rest at $x=1$. At what other position does the particle come to rest?
questions.answer: $v=0$: $20x-14x^2-6=0\Rightarrow7x^2-10x+3=0\Rightarrow(7x-3)(x-1)=0$, so $x=1$ or $x=\frac37$. The other position is $x=\frac37$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int_1^2\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{-2+3x-x^2}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$-2+3x-x^2=\frac14-\left(x-\frac32\right)^2$. Also $x+1=-\frac12(3-2x)+\frac52$, and $\dfrac d{dx}\left(-2+3x-x^2\right)=3-2x$.
$$\int_1^2\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{-2+3x-x^2}}dx=-\frac12\int_1^2\frac{3-2x}{\sqrt{-2+3x-x^2}}dx+\frac52\int_1^2\frac{dx}{\sqrt{\frac14-\left(x-\frac32\right)^2}}$$
$$=-\left[\sqrt{-2+3x-x^2}\right]_1^2+\frac52\left[\sin^{-1}(2x-3)\right]_1^2=-(0-0)+\frac52\left(\sin^{-1}1-\sin^{-1}(-1)\right)=\frac52\cdot\pi=\frac{5\pi}2.$$

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Show that the position vector of the point on the line $\mathbf r$ closest to the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is $\dfrac{x_0+2y_0+z_0}6\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
Let $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $P=(x_0,y_0,z_0)$. The closest point $Q=\lambda\mathbf d$ on the line is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$, so $(\overrightarrow{OP}-\lambda\mathbf d)\cdot\mathbf d=0$. Hence
$$\lambda=\frac{\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf d}=\frac{x_0+2y_0+z_0}{1+4+1}=\frac{x_0+2y_0+z_0}6,$$
so $Q=\dfrac{x_0+2y_0+z_0}6\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Consider the line $\mathbf r=\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$. The closest point on $\mathbf r$ to the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is $\dfrac{x_0+2y_0+z_0}6\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

Hence, or otherwise, find the point on the line $\mathbf r$ that is closest to a second line $\mathbf s=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}$, where $t\in(-\infty,\infty)$.
questions.answer:
A point on $\mathbf s$ is $P_t=(4-t,\,1+t,\,5t)$. By part (i), the closest point on $\mathbf r$ to $P_t$ has
$$\lambda=\frac{(4-t)+2(1+t)+5t}6=\frac{6+6t}6=1+t.$$
The squared distance from $P_t$ to the line $\mathbf r$ is then
$$d^2=(4-t-(1+t))^2+(1+t-2(1+t))^2+(5t-(1+t))^2=(3-2t)^2+(1+t)^2+(4t-1)^2=21t^2-18t+11.$$
$\dfrac{d(d^2)}{dt}=42t-18=0\Rightarrow t=\frac37$, a minimum since $\dfrac{d^2(d^2)}{dt^2}=42>0$. Then $\lambda=1+\frac37=\frac{10}7$.

The closest point on $\mathbf r$ is $\dfrac{10}7\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{10}7\\\frac{20}7\\\frac{10}7\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question:
In the diagram, the graph of $y=\dfrac1{\sqrt x}$ has been drawn, and $n$ rectangles have been constructed between $x=n$ and $x=2n$, each of width $1$ unit.

Show that $\displaystyle\int_n^{2n}\frac{dx}{\sqrt x}=2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)$.
questions.answer: $$\int_n^{2n}x^{-\frac12}dx=\Big[2\sqrt x\Big]_n^{2n}=2\sqrt{2n}-2\sqrt n=2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right).\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
In the diagram, the graph of $y=\dfrac1{\sqrt x}$ has been drawn, and $n$ rectangles of width $1$ unit have been constructed between $x=n$ and $x=2n$. Let $S_n=\dfrac1{\sqrt{n+1}}+\dfrac1{\sqrt{n+2}}+\dots+\dfrac1{\sqrt{2n}}$, and recall $\displaystyle\int_n^{2n}\frac{dx}{\sqrt x}=2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)$.

Show that $$2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)+\frac{1-\sqrt2}{\sqrt{2n}}<S_n<2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right).$$
questions.answer:
The rectangles drawn under the curve (the 'lower' rectangles, whose right-hand corner touches the curve) have heights $\frac1{\sqrt{n+1}},\dots,\frac1{\sqrt{2n}}$ and total area $S_n$. The upper rectangles (left-hand corner on the curve) have heights $\frac1{\sqrt n},\frac1{\sqrt{n+1}},\dots,\frac1{\sqrt{2n-1}}$ and total area $\frac1{\sqrt n}+S_n-\frac1{\sqrt{2n}}$.

Since $y=\frac1{\sqrt x}$ is decreasing, lower rectangles $<$ area under the curve $<$ upper rectangles:
$$S_n<2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)<\frac1{\sqrt n}+S_n-\frac1{\sqrt{2n}}.$$
The left inequality is the required upper bound. The right inequality gives
$$S_n>2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)-\frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac1{\sqrt{2n}}=2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)-\frac{\sqrt2-1}{\sqrt{2n}}=2\sqrt n\left(\sqrt2-1\right)+\frac{1-\sqrt2}{\sqrt{2n}},$$
using $\frac1{\sqrt n}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt{2n}}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: A particle's movement is represented by the vector $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t+t^{-1}\\t^3+t^{-3}\end{pmatrix}$, where $t\in\mathbb R^+$. Sketch the Cartesian graph that shows the path the particle can move along.
questions.answer:
$x=t+\frac1t$, $y=t^3+\frac1{t^3}$. Cubing, $x^3=t^3+3t+\frac3t+\frac1{t^3}=y+3x$, so
$$y=x^3-3x=x(x-\sqrt3)(x+\sqrt3).$$
For $t>0$, $x=t+\frac1t\ge2$ (AM–GM, equality at $t=1$), so the path is only the part of this cubic with $x\ge2$, starting at $(2,2)$ and rising to the right (each point is reached twice, by $t$ and $\frac1t$). The rest of the cubic (dashed) is not part of the path.

questions.question:
A particle $A$ of mass $m$ falls vertically from rest at a height $h$ above the ground. It is subject to a resistance $mkv$ where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$.

Show that $\ddot x=k(U-v)$, where $U$ is the terminal speed of the particle.
questions.answer: Taking downwards as positive: $m\ddot x=mg-mkv$, so $\ddot x=g-kv$. At terminal speed $\ddot x=0$, so $U=\dfrac gk$ and $g=kU$. Hence $\ddot x=kU-kv=k(U-v)$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
A particle $A$ of mass $m$ falls vertically from rest at a height $h$ above the ground. It is subject to a resistance $mkv$ where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$.

Prove that the speed of particle $A$ at any time $t$ is given by $v=U\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dv}{dt}=k(U-v)\Rightarrow\displaystyle\int_0^v\frac{dv}{U-v}=\int_0^tk\,dt$ (note $v<U$).
$$\Big[-\ln(U-v)\Big]_0^v=kt\ \Rightarrow\ \ln\frac U{U-v}=kt\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{U-v}U=e^{-kt}\ \Rightarrow\ v=U\left(1-e^{-kt}\right).\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
A particle $A$ of mass $m$ falls vertically from rest at a height $h$ above the ground. It is subject to a resistance $mkv$ where $v$ is its speed and $k$ is a positive constant. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$.

At the same time as particle $A$ falls from rest, another particle $B$ of mass $m$ is projected upwards in the same vertical line from the ground with a speed of $kU$, where $U$ is the terminal speed of the particle. Hence it can be shown that for particle $B$ its speed (upwards) at any time $t$ is given by $v=kUe^{-kt}-U\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)$. (Do NOT prove this.)

If the two particles collide after time $T$ seconds when particle $A$ has fallen a distance $X$, prove that
$$T=\frac1k\log_e\left(\frac U{U-h}\right).$$
questions.answer:
For $A$ (from $v=U(1-e^{-kt})$): $X=\displaystyle\int_0^TU\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)dt$.

For $B$ (starting at the ground), its height at time $T$ is
$$x_B=\int_0^T\left[kUe^{-kt}-U\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)\right]dt=\int_0^TkUe^{-kt}dt-X=U\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)-X.$$
At the collision, $A$ is at height $h-X$ and $B$ is at height $x_B$, so $h-X=x_B$:
$$h-X=U\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)-X\ \Rightarrow\ h=U\left(1-e^{-kT}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ e^{-kT}=\frac{U-h}U.$$
$$T=-\frac1k\ln\frac{U-h}U=\frac1k\ln\frac U{U-h}.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question: Consider the statement: *If an animal can fly, then it is a bird.* Which of the following is the contrapositive of this statement?
questions.answer: The contrapositive of 'if $P$ then $Q$' is 'if not $Q$ then not $P$': if an animal is not a bird, then it cannot fly (A).
options: If an animal is not a bird, then it cannot fly.
If an animal is a bird, then it can fly.
If an animal can fly, then it is not a bird.
If an animal cannot fly, then it is not a bird.

questions.question: What is the equation of the line which passes through $A(4,6,5)$ and $B(-2,3,-1)$?
questions.answer: Direction $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-2-4,\,3-6,\,-1-5)=(-6,-3,-6)$, and the line passes through $A$, so $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\6\\5\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-3\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ (D).

questions.question: Consider the proposition: *If a positive integer is not a perfect square, then it is not prime.* A counterexample to this proposition is to be found. A number with which of the following properties would suffice?
questions.answer: A counterexample to 'if $P$ then $Q$' makes $P$ true and $Q$ false: not a perfect square, and prime (A), e.g. $2$.
options: A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is not prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is not prime.

questions.question: A particle is moving in simple harmonic motion in a straight line with an amplitude of $3$ metres. When the particle is $2$ metres from the centre of motion, its speed is $5$ m/s. What is the period of the motion?
questions.answer: $v^2=n^2(A^2-x^2)\Rightarrow25=n^2(9-4)\Rightarrow n=\sqrt5$. Period $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{2\sqrt5\pi}{5}$ (B).

questions.question: The roots of the cubic equation $f(x)=0$ are $\alpha,\beta$ and $\gamma$. Which of the following cubic equations has roots $2\alpha+1$, $2\beta+1$ and $2\gamma+1$?
questions.answer: If $x=2\alpha+1$ then $\alpha=\dfrac{x-1}{2}$, and $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, so the new equation is $f\!\left(\dfrac{x-1}{2}\right)=0$ (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows the complex number $z=x+iy$, which lies in the third quadrant such that $x<y$. Given that $z^2=a+ib$, which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer: $z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2xyi$. In the third quadrant $x<0$ and $y<0$, so $xy>0$ and $b=2xy>0$. Since $x<y<0$, $|x|>|y|$, so $a=x^2-y^2>0$ (D).

questions.question: Consider the position vector of a particle $\mathbf r=t^2\mathbf i+2\cos t\,\mathbf j+2\sin t\,\mathbf k$. Which of the following best describes the motion of the particle?
questions.answer: The $\mathbf j,\mathbf k$ components $(2\cos t,2\sin t)$ describe a circle of radius $2$ about the $x$ axis, traversed anticlockwise (viewed from the positive $x$ side). The $x$ component $t^2$ has increasing speed, so the particle advances along the axis at an increasing rate (B).
options: Spiralling at an increasing rate about the $z$ axis in an anticlockwise direction.
Spiralling at an increasing rate about the $x$ axis in an anticlockwise direction.
Spiralling at an increasing rate about the $x$ axis in a clockwise direction.
Spiralling at a constant rate about the $x$ axis in an anticlockwise direction.

questions.question: Consider triangle $AOB$, where $A$ is the point $(1,0,1)$ and $B$ is the point $(0,2,2)$. Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: $OA=\sqrt2$, $OB=\sqrt8$, $AB=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$. Since $OA^2+AB^2=8=OB^2$, the right angle is at $A$. Then $\tan\angle AOB=\dfrac{AB}{OA}=\sqrt3$, so $\angle AOB=60^\circ$ and $\angle OBA=30^\circ$: $\angle AOB=2\angle OBA$ (D).
options: $\angle OAB$ is twice the size of $\angle OBA$
$\angle AOB$ is twice the size of $\angle OBA$

questions.question: Consider the complex equation $z^3=-p^3i$, where $p$ is a positive real number. What is the sum of all of the imaginary parts of all of the solutions that have a negative principal argument?
questions.answer: $-p^3i=p^3\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\tfrac\pi2\right)$, so $z=p\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\tfrac\pi6+\tfrac{2k\pi}3\right)$: arguments $-\tfrac\pi6,\ \tfrac\pi2,\ -\tfrac{5\pi}6$. The two negative arguments give imaginary parts $-\tfrac p2$ and $-\tfrac p2$, a sum of $-p$ (D). (The question asks for a sum of imaginary parts, which is real, so $-p$ not $-pi$.)

questions.question: A unit mass is projected horizontally from the top of a tall building. Air resistance is $\mathbf R$ and the gravitational force is $\mathbf G$. The position vector of the mass is $\mathbf r$, with the origin at the base of the building, and the velocity vector is $\mathbf v$. At the point $P$ (see diagram), $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v=0$. Which of the following is consistent with the motion of the particle at $P$?
questions.answer: Each fraction is the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Resistance opposes the velocity, so $\cos(\mathbf R,\mathbf v)=-1$. Gravity points down and $\mathbf r$ points up-and-across from the base, so $\cos(\mathbf G,\mathbf r)$ is negative. Since $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v=0$ and $\mathbf R$ is parallel to $-\mathbf v$, $\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf r=0$. Gravity has a component along the downward-moving velocity, so $\cos(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)>0$. Thus $-1<\cos(\mathbf G,\mathbf r)<0=\cos(\mathbf R,\mathbf r)<\cos(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$, which is option A.
options: $\dfrac{\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf R||\mathbf v|}<\dfrac{\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r}{|\mathbf G||\mathbf r|}<\dfrac{\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf r}{|\mathbf R||\mathbf r|}<\dfrac{\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf G||\mathbf v|}$

$\dfrac{\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r}{|\mathbf G||\mathbf r|}<\dfrac{\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf G||\mathbf v|}<\dfrac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf R}{|\mathbf v||\mathbf R|}<\dfrac{\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf r}{|\mathbf R||\mathbf r|}$

$\dfrac{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf R}{|\mathbf r||\mathbf R|}<\dfrac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf G}{|\mathbf v||\mathbf G|}<\dfrac{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf G}{|\mathbf r||\mathbf G|}<\dfrac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf R}{|\mathbf v||\mathbf R|}$

$\dfrac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf G}{|\mathbf v||\mathbf G|}<\dfrac{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf G}{|\mathbf r||\mathbf G|}<\dfrac{\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf R||\mathbf v|}<\dfrac{\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf R}{|\mathbf r||\mathbf R|}$

questions.question: Consider the vector $\mathbf r=p\mathbf i-4\mathbf j+5\mathbf k$. If $\mathbf r$ has a magnitude of $5\sqrt2$ units, what are the exact value(s) of $p$?
questions.answer: $p^2+16+25=50\Rightarrow p^2=9\Rightarrow p=\pm3$.

questions.question: Find the size of the angle between the vectors $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, giving your answer correct to the nearest minute.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=3+4-2=5$, $|\mathbf a|=3$, $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt{14}$.
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{3\sqrt{14}}$, so $\theta=63^\circ33'$.

questions.question: Sketch the region in the complex plane where the inequalities $|z-i|\le1$ and $0\le\arg(z-i)\le\dfrac\pi3$ hold simultaneously.
questions.answer: $|z-i|\le1$ is the closed disc of radius $1$ centred at $i$. $0\le\arg(z-i)\le\frac\pi3$ is the region between the horizontal ray from $i$ to the right and the ray from $i$ at $60^\circ$ above it (the centre $i$ itself excluded, as $\arg 0$ is undefined). The region is the circular sector of radius $1$ centred at $i$ between these two rays, with the boundary arcs and rays included but the point $i$ excluded.

questions.question: Show that, if $a$ and $b$ are positive integers, then $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2$.
questions.answer: $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba-2=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-2ab}{ab}=\dfrac{(a-b)^2}{ab}\ge0$ since $(a-b)^2\ge0$ and $ab>0$. Hence $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2$.

questions.question: The complex number $z^2$ is shown on the diagram. Given that $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant, find $z$ in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer:
From the diagram $z^2=4\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)$. Then $z=\pm2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\tfrac\pi3\right)$, i.e. $2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\tfrac\pi3\right)$ or $2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)$. The fourth quadrant solution is
$$z=2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac\pi3\right).$$

questions.question: Consider the equation $(p+5)^{36}+(p+3)^{35}=7$. Give reasons as to why there is no integer root $p$ for the equation.
questions.answer:
If $p$ is odd, $p+5$ and $p+3$ are both even, so both terms are even and their sum is even.
If $p$ is even, $p+5$ and $p+3$ are both odd, so both terms are odd and their sum is even.
In either case the left side is even, but $7$ is odd, so there is no integer root.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int x\ln x\,dx$.
questions.answer: By parts with $u=\ln x$, $dv=x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int x\ln x\,dx=\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x-\int\frac x2\,dx=\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x-\frac{x^2}{4}+c$.

questions.question: Find $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $\dfrac{x}{(x-2)^2(x-1)}=\dfrac{A}{x-2}+\dfrac{B}{(x-2)^2}+\dfrac{C}{x-1}$.
Hence, show that $\displaystyle\int_3^4\frac{x}{(x-2)^2(x-1)}\,dx=\ln\!\left(\frac34\right)+1$.
questions.answer:
$\displaystyle\int_3^4\left[\frac{-1}{x-2}+\frac2{(x-2)^2}+\frac1{x-1}\right]dx=\left[\ln\frac{x-1}{x-2}-\frac{2}{x-2}\right]_3^4$
$=\left(\ln\tfrac32-1\right)-\left(\ln2-2\right)=\ln\tfrac32-\ln2+1=\ln\tfrac34+1$.

prev.question: Find $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $\dfrac{x}{(x-2)^2(x-1)}=\dfrac{A}{x-2}+\dfrac{B}{(x-2)^2}+\dfrac{C}{x-1}$.

questions.question: Consider the statement $P$: *If $2n^2+3n+1$ is even, then $n$ is odd.* Prove that the converse of $P$ is true.
questions.answer:
The converse is: if $n$ is odd, then $2n^2+3n+1$ is even.
Let $n=2k+1$. Then $2n^2+3n+1=2(4k^2+4k+1)+6k+3+1=8k^2+14k+6=2(4k^2+7k+3)$, which is even. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Factorise $P(z)=z^4-6z^3+18z^2-14z-39$, given that one of the zeros of $P(z)$ is $2-3i$.
questions.answer:
$P$ has real coefficients, so $2+3i$ is also a zero. The quadratic factor is $z^2-4z+13$. Dividing, $P(z)=(z^2-4z+13)(z^2-2z-3)=(z^2-4z+13)(z+1)(z-3)$.
$$P(z)=(z+1)(z-3)(z^2-4z+13)$$ (zeros $-1,\ 3,\ 2\pm3i$).

questions.question: Consider the complex number $z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. Show that $\phi=\dfrac{2z}{z^2+|z|^2}$ is purely real.
questions.answer: $|z|^2=z\bar z$, so $\phi=\dfrac{2z}{z^2+z\bar z}=\dfrac{2z}{z(z+\bar z)}=\dfrac{2}{z+\bar z}=\dfrac{2}{2\operatorname{Re}(z)}=\dfrac1{r\cos\theta}$, which is real. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{2x}-e^x}{e^x+1}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $u=e^x$, $du=e^x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int\frac{u-1}{u+1}\,du=\int\left(1-\frac2{u+1}\right)du=u-2\ln(u+1)+c$.
$$=e^x-2\ln(e^x+1)+c$$

questions.question: For positive real numbers $a$ and $b$, $a\ne b$, it is given that $a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$ and $(a-b)^2>0$. Using these facts, or otherwise, prove that $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$.
questions.answer: $a^3+b^3-ab(a+b)=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)-ab(a+b)=(a+b)(a-b)^2>0$, since $a+b>0$ and $(a-b)^2>0$. Hence $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Hence, or otherwise, show that if $c$ is also a positive real number not equal to $a$ or $b$, then $2(a^3+b^3+c^3)>a^2(b+c)+b^2(a+c)+c^2(a+b)$.
questions.answer:
From part (i) applied to each pair:
$a^3+b^3>a^2b+ab^2$, $\ b^3+c^3>b^2c+bc^2$, $\ a^3+c^3>a^2c+ac^2$.
Adding: $2(a^3+b^3+c^3)>a^2(b+c)+b^2(a+c)+c^2(a+b)$. $\blacksquare$

prev.question: For positive real numbers $a$ and $b$, $a\ne b$, it is given that $a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$ and $(a-b)^2>0$. Using these facts, or otherwise, prove that $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$.
prev.answer: $a^3+b^3-ab(a+b)=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)-ab(a+b)=(a+b)(a-b)^2>0$, since $a+b>0$ and $(a-b)^2>0$. Hence $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: A particle moves along the $x$ axis in simple harmonic motion. Its displacement $x$ cm from the origin at time $t$ seconds is $x=5-4\cos^22\pi t$. Find the centre and the amplitude of the motion.
questions.answer:
$\cos^22\pi t=\dfrac{1+\cos4\pi t}{2}$, so $x=5-2-2\cos4\pi t=3-2\cos4\pi t$.
The centre of motion is $x=3$ cm and the amplitude is $2$ cm.

questions.question: For the particle in part (i), $x=3-2\cos4\pi t$. Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $5$ seconds.
questions.answer: The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi}=\dfrac12$ s, so in $5$ s there are $10$ complete oscillations. Each oscillation covers $4\times2=8$ cm, so the distance is $10\times8=80$ cm.

prev.question: A particle moves along the $x$ axis in simple harmonic motion. Its displacement $x$ cm from the origin at time $t$ seconds is $x=5-4\cos^22\pi t$. Find the centre and the amplitude of the motion.
prev.answer:
$\cos^22\pi t=\dfrac{1+\cos4\pi t}{2}$, so $x=5-2-2\cos4\pi t=3-2\cos4\pi t$.
The centre of motion is $x=3$ cm and the amplitude is $2$ cm.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that $P(x)=120+120x+60x^2+20x^3+5x^4+x^5$ has no double roots.
questions.answer:
Suppose $P$ has a double root $\alpha$, so $P(\alpha)=0$ and $P'(\alpha)=0$.
$P'(x)=120+120x+60x^2+20x^3+5x^4$, so $P(x)-P'(x)=x^5$.
Then $\alpha^5=P(\alpha)-P'(\alpha)=0$, so $\alpha=0$. But $P(0)=120\ne0$, a contradiction. Hence $P$ has no double roots. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Let $z=1+i$ and $w=-\sqrt3+i$. Find $zw$ in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer: $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi4$, $w=2\operatorname{cis}\frac{5\pi}6$. $zw=2\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(\frac\pi4+\frac{5\pi}6\right)=2\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\frac{13\pi}{12}=2\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac{11\pi}{12}\right)$.

questions.question: Let $z=1+i$ and $w=-\sqrt3+i$. Hence show that $\cos\!\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$.
questions.answer:
Directly, $zw=(1+i)(-\sqrt3+i)=-\sqrt3-1+i(1-\sqrt3)=-(1+\sqrt3)+i(1-\sqrt3)$.
Equating real parts with $2\sqrt2\cos\!\left(-\frac{11\pi}{12}\right)=-2\sqrt2\cos\frac\pi{12}$:
$$\cos\frac\pi{12}=\frac{1+\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}{4}.\ \blacksquare$$

An $80$ kg mass is dragged along a horizontal surface by a force of $100$ N, and is subject to friction of $0.1v$ newtons, where $v$ is its speed in m/s. The mass is initially at rest. The equation of motion is $\ddot x=\dfrac{1000-v}{800}$ (do not prove this). Show that $t=800\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1000}{1000-v}\right)$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{1000-v}{800}\Rightarrow t=800\displaystyle\int\frac{dv}{1000-v}=-800\ln(1000-v)+C$.
$t=0,\ v=0$: $C=800\ln1000$. So $t=800\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1000}{1000-v}\right)$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: The vectors $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are defined as $\mathbf u=\mathbf a+m\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf v=m\mathbf a-\mathbf b$, where $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are unit vectors and $m$ is a real constant. Given that $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=1$, and that the acute angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is $\dfrac\pi3$, find the value(s) of $m$.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12$.
$\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=m|\mathbf a|^2-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+m^2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b-m|\mathbf b|^2=m-\frac12+\frac{m^2}2-m=\frac{m^2-1}{2}$.
$\frac{m^2-1}2=1\Rightarrow m^2=3\Rightarrow m=\pm\sqrt3$.

questions.question: Two masses $M$ kg and $(4M+12)$ kg are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string passing over a pulley. The mass $M$ kg accelerates upwards at $3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ while the $(4M+12)$ kg mass moves down a smooth plane inclined at $30^\circ$ (see diagram). Take $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find $M$.
questions.answer:
Let $T$ be the tension. For $M$: $T-10M=3M\Rightarrow T=13M$.
For the other mass along the slope: $(4M+12)(10)\sin30^\circ-T=3(4M+12)$.
$5(4M+12)-13M=3(4M+12)\Rightarrow2(4M+12)=13M\Rightarrow5M=24$.
$$M=4.8\text{ kg}$$

questions.question: A spiral starts at the origin and completes two clockwise turns to end at $(0,2\pi)$ (see diagram). Its position from $t=0$ to $t=T$ is given by $x=f(t)$, $y=g(t)$. Find $f(t)$, $g(t)$ and $T$.
questions.answer:
The radius grows linearly from $0$ to $2\pi$ over two turns, and the spiral is clockwise starting from the $y$-axis direction, so with angle $t$ and radius $\frac t2$:
$$f(t)=\frac t2\sin t,\qquad g(t)=\frac t2\cos t,\qquad T=4\pi.$$
Check: at $t=4\pi$, $f=0$ and $g=2\pi$.

questions.question: The spiral in part (i) is $x=\frac t2\sin t$, $y=\frac t2\cos t$ for $t\in[0,4\pi]$. A second spiral has $x=g(t)=\frac t2\cos t$, $y=f(t)=\frac t2\sin t$ for $t\in[0,\frac T2]=[0,2\pi]$. If the second spiral were drawn on the same axes, how many points of intersection would it have with the first spiral?
questions.answer: The second spiral is the reflection of the first (restricted to its first turn) in the line $y=x$, so intersections lie on $y=x$ (or are symmetric pairs). Counting from the diagram gives $3$ points of intersection: the origin, and the points at $t=\frac\pi4$ and $t=\frac{5\pi}4$ on the line $y=x$.

questions.question: Consider $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt x\,(1-x)^n\,dx$, $n=0,1,2,3,\dots$ Show that $I_n=\dfrac{2n}{2n+3}I_{n-1}$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$
questions.answer:
By parts with $u=(1-x)^n$, $dv=\sqrt x\,dx$, $v=\frac23x^{3/2}$:
$I_n=\left[\frac23x^{3/2}(1-x)^n\right]_0^1+\frac{2n}3\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{3/2}(1-x)^{n-1}dx$. The boundary term is $0$.
Write $x^{3/2}=\sqrt x\,[1-(1-x)]$: $I_n=\frac{2n}3\left(I_{n-1}-I_n\right)$.
$\left(1+\frac{2n}3\right)I_n=\frac{2n}3I_{n-1}\Rightarrow I_n=\dfrac{2n}{2n+3}I_{n-1}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: With $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt x\,(1-x)^n\,dx$ and $I_n=\dfrac{2n}{2n+3}I_{n-1}$, evaluate $I_1$.
questions.answer: $I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt x\,dx=\frac23$, so $I_1=\dfrac25\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac4{15}$.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is released and allowed to fall vertically in a medium in which the resistance is $mk$ times the square of the velocity $v$ of the particle. Write an equation for the acceleration of the particle in terms of $v$.
questions.answer: Taking downwards as positive: $m\ddot x=mg-mkv^2$, so $\ddot x=g-kv^2$.

questions.question: A particle falls vertically from rest with acceleration $\ddot x=g-kv^2$. Show that the terminal velocity is $V_T=\sqrt{\dfrac gk}$.
questions.answer: At terminal velocity $\ddot x=0$: $g-kV_T^2=0\Rightarrow V_T=\sqrt{\dfrac gk}$ (taking the positive root as the particle falls downwards). $\blacksquare$

questions.question: The line $L$ with equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\6\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ intersects the sphere $(x+1)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-3)^2=45$ at two points $A$ and $B$. Find the shortest distance between the centre of the sphere $C$ and the chord $AB$.
questions.answer:
On $L$: $x+1=\lambda$, $y-2=2\lambda$, $z-3=3+\lambda$. Substituting: $\lambda^2+4\lambda^2+(3+\lambda)^2=45\Rightarrow\lambda^2+\lambda-6=0\Rightarrow\lambda=2$ or $-3$.
$A(1,6,8)$ and $B(-4,-4,3)$. The centre is $C(-1,2,3)$ and the midpoint of $AB$ is $M\!\left(-\tfrac32,1,\tfrac{11}2\right)$.
The shortest distance from $C$ to the chord is $CM$: $\overrightarrow{CM}=\left(-\tfrac12,-1,\tfrac52\right)$, $|CM|=\sqrt{\tfrac14+1+\tfrac{25}4}=\dfrac{\sqrt{30}}2$.

questions.question: Given $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2a_n}$ and $a_1=1$, prove by mathematical induction that for all integers $n\ge1$, $a_n=2^{\left(1-2^{(1-n)}\right)}$.
questions.answer:
**Base case** $n=1$: $a_1=2^{1-2^0}=2^0=1$. ✓
**Assume** $a_k=2^{1-2^{1-k}}$ for some $k\ge1$.
**Then** $a_{k+1}=\sqrt{2\cdot2^{1-2^{1-k}}}=\left(2^{2-2^{1-k}}\right)^{1/2}=2^{1-2^{-k}}=2^{1-2^{1-(k+1)}}$.
So the result holds for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all integers $n\ge1$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Use de Moivre's theorem to express $\cos4\theta$ in terms of $\cos\theta$.
questions.answer:
$\cos4\theta+i\sin4\theta=(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^4$. Real part: $\cos^4\theta-6\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta+\sin^4\theta=\cos^4\theta-6\cos^2\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)+(1-\cos^2\theta)^2$
$$\cos4\theta=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1$$

questions.question: Use $\cos4\theta=8\cos^4\theta-8\cos^2\theta+1$ to solve the equation $8x^4-8x^2+1=0$.
questions.answer:
Let $x=\cos\theta$: the equation is $\cos4\theta=0$, so $4\theta=\frac\pi2+k\pi$, $\theta=\frac\pi8,\frac{3\pi}8,\frac{5\pi}8,\frac{7\pi}8$.
$$x=\cos\frac\pi8,\ \cos\frac{3\pi}8,\ \cos\frac{5\pi}8,\ \cos\frac{7\pi}8$$

questions.question: $M$ and $P$ are points with position vectors $\overrightarrow{OM}=\mathbf m$ and $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf p$. $N$ is the midpoint of $MP$ and has position vector $\overrightarrow{ON}=\mathbf n$. $PQ$ is perpendicular to $MN$ and $\overrightarrow{NQ}=\lambda\overrightarrow{ON}$. Show that $\lambda=\dfrac{|\mathbf m|^2+|\mathbf n|^2-2\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}{|\mathbf n|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}$.
questions.answer:
$N$ is the midpoint, so $\mathbf p=2\mathbf n-\mathbf m$. $\overrightarrow{MN}=\mathbf n-\mathbf m$.
$\overrightarrow{OQ}=\mathbf n+\lambda\mathbf n=(1+\lambda)\mathbf n$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(1+\lambda)\mathbf n-(2\mathbf n-\mathbf m)=(\lambda-1)\mathbf n+\mathbf m$.
$PQ\perp MN$: $[(\lambda-1)\mathbf n+\mathbf m]\cdot(\mathbf n-\mathbf m)=0$
$(\lambda-1)|\mathbf n|^2-(\lambda-1)\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n+\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n-|\mathbf m|^2=0$
$(\lambda-1)\left(|\mathbf n|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n\right)=|\mathbf m|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n$
$\lambda=1+\dfrac{|\mathbf m|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}{|\mathbf n|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}=\dfrac{|\mathbf m|^2+|\mathbf n|^2-2\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}{|\mathbf n|^2-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf n}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Evaluate $\left(\sqrt3+i\right)^8$.
questions.answer: $\sqrt3+i=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi6$, so $(\sqrt3+i)^8=2^8\operatorname{cis}\frac{8\pi}6=256\operatorname{cis}\frac{4\pi}3=256\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac{2\pi}3\right)$ (D).

questions.question: Which of these algebraic fractions cannot be written as partial fractions in the form $\dfrac{a}{x+b}+\dfrac{c}{x-d}$, where $a,b,c$ and $d$ are real numbers?
questions.answer: This form needs the denominator to factorise into two distinct real linear factors. $x^2-4x+8=(x-2)^2+4$ has no real roots, so it cannot be factorised over $\mathbb R$ (B). ($x^2-8x+16=(x-4)^2$ is a repeated factor; the fraction $\frac{2x-8}{(x-4)^2}$ simplifies to $\frac{2}{x-4}$, which fits the form with $a=0$.) *(The school's worked key labels this answer 'C', but with the options as printed, the fraction with $x^2-4x+8$ is option B.)*

questions.question: Consider the complex number $z=a+ib$ (where $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $a\ne0$, $b\ne0$) and its complex conjugate $\bar z$. Which row of the table correctly classifies the sum, difference, product and quotient of $z$ and $\bar z$?
questions.answer: $z+\bar z=2a$ (real); $z-\bar z=2ib$ (imaginary); $z\bar z=a^2+b^2$ (real); $\dfrac z{\bar z}=\dfrac{(a+ib)^2}{a^2+b^2}=\dfrac{a^2-b^2+2abi}{a^2+b^2}$, which is complex since $a,b\ne0$ (C).
options: $z+\bar z$ Real; $z-\bar z$ Imaginary; $z\bar z$ Real; $z\div\bar z$ Imaginary
$z+\bar z$ Complex; $z-\bar z$ Real; $z\bar z$ Complex; $z\div\bar z$ Real
$z+\bar z$ Real; $z-\bar z$ Imaginary; $z\bar z$ Real; $z\div\bar z$ Complex
$z+\bar z$ Real; $z-\bar z$ Real; $z\bar z$ Imaginary; $z\div\bar z$ Complex

questions.question: A vector makes an angle of $\dfrac\pi4$ with the positive direction of the $x$-axis, and an angle of $\dfrac\pi4$ with the positive direction of the $y$-axis. What angle does the vector make with the positive direction of the $z$-axis?
questions.answer: The direction cosines satisfy $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1$: $\frac12+\frac12+\cos^2\gamma=1$, so $\cos\gamma=0$ and the angle is $\dfrac\pi2$ (C).

questions.question: Consider $\triangle AOB$, where $A$ is the point $(1,0,1)$ and $B$ is the point $(0,2,2)$ (see diagram). Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: $OA=\sqrt2$, $OB=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$, $AB=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$. Since $OA^2+AB^2=OB^2$, the right angle is at $A$ (so A is false, and no two sides are equal). $\tan\angle AOB=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt3$ gives $\angle AOB=60^\circ$ and $\angle OBA=30^\circ$, so $\angle AOB=2\angle OBA$ (D).

questions.question: Which of the following is equivalent to the expression $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2}{(25-x^2)\sqrt{25-x^2}}\,dx$?

questions.question: Find the vector projection of $\mathbf v=4\mathbf i+5\mathbf j-\mathbf k$ onto $\mathbf u=\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u=4-10-3=-9$, $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=14$.
$$\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\mathbf u=-\frac9{14}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}$$

questions.question: Find the fourth roots of $8+8\sqrt3\,i$.
questions.answer:
$|8+8\sqrt3i|=\sqrt{64+192}=16$, $\arg=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\frac\pi3$, so $8+8\sqrt3i=16\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$.
Let $z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta$: $r^4=16\Rightarrow r=2$, $4\theta=\frac\pi3+2k\pi\Rightarrow\theta=\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}2$.
$$z=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi{12},\ 2\operatorname{cis}\frac{7\pi}{12},\ 2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac{11\pi}{12}\right),\ 2\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)$$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{6x-5-x^2}}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $6x-5-x^2=4-(x-3)^2$, so $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2^2-(x-3)^2}}=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-3}{2}\right)+c$.

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to prove that $n^2\ge2n+1$ for all integers $n\ge3$.
questions.answer:
**Base case** $n=3$: $9\ge7$. ✓
**Assume** $k^2\ge2k+1$ for some $k\ge3$.
**Then** $(k+1)^2=k^2+2k+1\ge(2k+1)+2k+1=2(k+1)+2k\ge2(k+1)+1$ since $2k\ge1$.
So the result holds for $n=k+1$. By induction it is true for all integers $n\ge3$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int x(1-x)^7\,dx$.

The lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are given by $\ell_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\\ln a\\\ln a\end{pmatrix}$ and $\ell_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-3\\\ln a\\1\end{pmatrix}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $a$ is a constant. Given that $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are orthogonal (their direction vectors are perpendicular), find the value(s) of $a$.
questions.answer:
$\begin{pmatrix}2\\\ln a\\\ln a\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}-3\\\ln a\\1\end{pmatrix}=0\Rightarrow-6+(\ln a)^2+\ln a=0$.
Let $m=\ln a$: $m^2+m-6=(m-2)(m+3)=0$, so $m=2$ or $m=-3$.
$$a=e^2\quad\text{or}\quad a=e^{-3}$$ (both valid as $a>0$).

questions.question: Consider the line $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-7\\3\end{pmatrix}$. Find the equation of a line that meets $\mathbf r$ at right angles.
questions.answer:
The new line must pass through a point of $\mathbf r$ and have direction $\mathbf d=(a,b,c)$ with $\mathbf d\cdot(1,-7,3)=0$, i.e. $a-7b+3c=0$. Take $\mathbf d=(1,1,2)$: $1-7+6=0$ ✓.
Through the point $(0,1,2)$ (where $\mu=0$):
$$\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$$ (many answers are possible).

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int_3^4\frac{x}{(x-2)^2(x-1)}\,dx$.
For any complex numbers $\omega_1=a+bi$ and $\omega_2=c+di$ ($a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$), prove that $|\omega_1+\omega_2|^2+|\omega_1-\omega_2|^2=2\left(|\omega_1|^2+|\omega_2|^2\right)$.
What does the result $|\omega_1+\omega_2|^2+|\omega_1-\omega_2|^2=2\left(|\omega_1|^2+|\omega_2|^2\right)$ mean geometrically?
questions.answer: Represent $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ as adjacent sides of a parallelogram; $|\omega_1+\omega_2|$ and $|\omega_1-\omega_2|$ are the lengths of its diagonals. The result states that in a parallelogram, the sum of the squares of the diagonals equals the sum of the squares of the four sides.

prev.question: For any complex numbers $\omega_1=a+bi$ and $\omega_2=c+di$ ($a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$), prove that $|\omega_1+\omega_2|^2+|\omega_1-\omega_2|^2=2\left(|\omega_1|^2+|\omega_2|^2\right)$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int e^x\sin x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
By parts twice: $I=e^x\sin x-\int e^x\cos x\,dx=e^x\sin x-\left[e^x\cos x+\int e^x\sin x\,dx\right]=e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x-I$.
$$I=\tfrac12e^x(\sin x-\cos x)+c$$

questions.question: Prove or disprove the following statement: $\forall x:\ x=2k+1\ (k\in\mathbb Z),\ \exists a,b\in\mathbb Z:\ a^2-b^2=x$.
questions.answer:
The statement is **true**: every odd integer is a difference of two squares.
Given $x=2k+1$, take $a=k+1$ and $b=k$ (both integers). Then $a^2-b^2=(k+1)^2-k^2=2k+1=x$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Factorise $P(z)=z^4-6z^3+18z^2-14z-39$, given that one of the zeros of $P(z)$ is $2-3i$.
questions.answer:
$P$ has real coefficients, so $2+3i$ is also a zero, giving the factor $[z-(2-3i)][z-(2+3i)]=z^2-4z+13$. Dividing, $P(z)=(z^2-4z+13)(z^2-2z-3)$.
$$P(z)=(z-3)(z+1)\left(z-(2-3i)\right)\left(z-(2+3i)\right)$$

questions.question: Given a series defined by $T_0=0$ and $T_n=2T_{n-1}+1$ for $n\ge1$, use mathematical induction to prove that $T_n=2^n-1$ for all positive integers $n$.
questions.answer:
**Base case** $n=1$: $T_1=2T_0+1=1=2^1-1$. ✓
**Assume** $T_k=2^k-1$ for some $k\ge1$.
**Then** $T_{k+1}=2T_k+1=2(2^k-1)+1=2^{k+1}-1$.
So the result holds for $n=k+1$; by induction it is true for all positive integers $n$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: The new music building at a school is a cube of side length one unit surmounted by a right square pyramid, as shown. The roof is pitched at $45^\circ$: the triangular roof panels meet the flat ceiling at $45^\circ$. Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf c$ and $\overrightarrow{AE}=\mathbf e$. Express $\overrightarrow{FI}$ in terms of $\mathbf b$, $\mathbf c$ and/or $\mathbf e$.
questions.answer:
Let $K$ be the centre of the top face $EFGH$. A $45^\circ$ pitch over a horizontal run of $\tfrac12$ (from the midpoint of an edge to $K$) means the apex height is $KI=\tfrac12$, so $\overrightarrow{KI}=\tfrac12\mathbf e$.
$\overrightarrow{KF}=\overrightarrow{EF}-\overrightarrow{EK}=\mathbf b-\tfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)$.
$$\overrightarrow{FI}=\overrightarrow{KI}-\overrightarrow{KF}=\tfrac12\mathbf e-\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=\tfrac12(\mathbf e-\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$$

questions.question: In the building of part (i) (a unit cube $ABCDEFGH$ with pyramid apex $I$ above the centre $K$ of $EFGH$, $KI=\tfrac12$, with $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf c$, $\overrightarrow{AE}=\mathbf e$), find the size of $\angle FIH$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{IF}=\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf c-\mathbf e)$ and $\overrightarrow{IH}=\overrightarrow{KH}-\overrightarrow{KI}=\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)-\tfrac12\mathbf e=\tfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf b-\mathbf e)$. Since $\mathbf b,\mathbf c,\mathbf e$ are mutually perpendicular unit vectors:
$\overrightarrow{IF}\cdot\overrightarrow{IH}=\tfrac14(-1-1+1)=-\tfrac14$, and $|\overrightarrow{IF}|=|\overrightarrow{IH}|=\tfrac12\sqrt3$.
$\cos\angle FIH=\dfrac{-1/4}{3/4}=-\dfrac13\Rightarrow\angle FIH=109.47^\circ$ ($109^\circ28'$).

questions.question: A vertical flagpole is mounted at $I$ (the apex of the pyramid on the unit cube, whose pyramid has height $\tfrac12$), extending up to a point $T$. The length of the flagpole is chosen to be a third of the total height of the building, including the flagpole. Find $\overrightarrow{IT}$ in terms of $\mathbf e$.
questions.answer:
The building without the flagpole has height $1+\tfrac12=\tfrac32$. Let $IT=h\,\mathbf e$: $h=\tfrac13\left(\tfrac32+h\right)\Rightarrow2h=\tfrac32\Rightarrow h=\tfrac34$.
$$\overrightarrow{IT}=\tfrac34\mathbf e$$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{(x^2-1)^3}}{x}\,dx$, using the substitution $x=\sec\theta$, or otherwise.
questions.answer:
$x=\sec\theta$, $dx=\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$, $\sqrt{x^2-1}=\tan\theta$ (for $x>1$):
$\displaystyle\int\frac{\tan^3\theta}{\sec\theta}\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta=\int\tan^4\theta\,d\theta=\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\tan^2\theta\,d\theta=\int\sec^2\theta\tan^2\theta\,d\theta-\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta$
$=\tfrac13\tan^3\theta-\tan\theta+\theta+c$. With $\tan\theta=\sqrt{x^2-1}$ and $\theta=\sec^{-1}x$:
$$\frac13(x^2-1)^{3/2}-\sqrt{x^2-1}+\sec^{-1}x+c$$

questions.question: State the negation of *if the road is wet, it must have rained*.
questions.answer: $\neg(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv P\wedge\neg Q$: the road is wet **and** it did not rain.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^nx\,dx$, where $n$ is an integer and $n\ge3$. Show that $I_n+I_{n-2}=\dfrac1{n-1}$.
questions.answer:
$I_n+I_{n-2}=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\,(\tan^2x+1)\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\sec^2x\,dx$.
Let $u=\tan x$, $du=\sec^2x\,dx$; $x=0\to u=0$, $x=\frac\pi4\to u=1$:
$=\displaystyle\int_0^1u^{n-2}\,du=\left[\frac{u^{n-1}}{n-1}\right]_0^1=\frac1{n-1}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^nx\,dx$ with $I_n+I_{n-2}=\dfrac1{n-1}$ for $n\ge3$. Hence evaluate $I_7$.
questions.answer:
$I_7=\frac16-I_5=\frac16-\left(\frac14-I_3\right)=\frac16-\frac14+\left(\frac12-I_1\right)$.
$I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx=\Big[-\ln|\cos x|\Big]_0^{\pi/4}=-\ln\frac1{\sqrt2}=\frac12\ln2$.
$$I_7=\frac5{12}-\frac12\ln2$$

questions.question: The points $z_1=2(3+i)$ and $z_2=2(1+i)$ satisfy $\arg\!\left(\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=\dfrac\pi6$. Let $z=x+iy$, where $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Realise the denominator in the expression $\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}$.

With $z_1=2(3+i)$, $z_2=2(1+i)$ and $\arg\!\left(\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=\dfrac\pi6$, use the result $\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}=\dfrac{(x-6)(x-2)+(y-2)^2+4(y-2)\,i}{(x-2)^2+(y-2)^2}$ to show that $\left|z-\left\{4+2\left(1+\sqrt3\right)i\right\}\right|=4$.
questions.answer:
Since the argument is $\frac\pi6$, $\dfrac{\operatorname{Im}}{\operatorname{Re}}=\tan\frac\pi6=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ (with $\operatorname{Re}>0$). The denominators cancel:
$\sqrt3\cdot4(y-2)=(x-6)(x-2)+(y-2)^2$
$4\sqrt3y-8\sqrt3=x^2-8x+12+y^2-4y+4$
$x^2-8x+y^2-(4+4\sqrt3)\,y=-8\sqrt3-16$.
Complete the squares: $(x-4)^2+\left(y-(2+2\sqrt3)\right)^2=-8\sqrt3-16+16+(2+2\sqrt3)^2=-8\sqrt3+4+8\sqrt3+12=16$.
So $\left|z-\left\{4+2(1+\sqrt3)i\right\}\right|=4$. $\blacksquare$

prev.question: The points $z_1=2(3+i)$ and $z_2=2(1+i)$ satisfy $\arg\!\left(\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=\dfrac\pi6$. Let $z=x+iy$, where $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Realise the denominator in the expression $\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}$.

questions.question: Sketch on an Argand diagram the locus of $z$ satisfying $\arg\!\left(\dfrac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=\dfrac\pi6$, where $z_1=6+2i$ and $z_2=2+2i$.
questions.answer: From part (ii) the locus lies on the circle with centre $4+2(1+\sqrt3)i$ (the point $(4,\,2+2\sqrt3)\approx(4,5.46)$) and radius $4$, passing through $z_1$ and $z_2$. The chord $z_2z_1$ has length $4$ (equal to the radius) and subtends $60^\circ$ at the centre, so the inscribed angle is $\frac\pi6$ on the major arc. The locus is the **major arc** above the chord (the part of the circle above $\operatorname{Im}z=2$), with open circles at $z_1$ and $z_2$ since $\arg$ is undefined there.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{1+x-x^2}{1-x+x^2}$, where $0<x<1$. Without using calculus, prove that $1<f(x)\le\dfrac53$.
questions.answer:
The denominator $1-x+x^2=\left(x-\frac12\right)^2+\frac34>0$.
$f(x)-1=\dfrac{(1+x-x^2)-(1-x+x^2)}{1-x+x^2}=\dfrac{2x(1-x)}{1-x+x^2}>0$ since $0<x<1$. So $f(x)>1$.
$\dfrac53-f(x)=\dfrac{5(1-x+x^2)-3(1+x-x^2)}{3(1-x+x^2)}=\dfrac{8x^2-8x+2}{3(1-x+x^2)}=\dfrac{2(2x-1)^2}{3(1-x+x^2)}\ge0$. So $f(x)\le\frac53$.
Hence $1<f(x)\le\frac53$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to prove that $3^{2n^2}-1$ is divisible by $8$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ge1$).
questions.answer:
**Base case** $n=1$: $3^2-1=8$, divisible by $8$. ✓
**Assume** $3^{2k^2}-1=8M$ for some integer $M$ and $k\ge1$, i.e. $3^{2k^2}=8M+1$.
**Then** $3^{2(k+1)^2}=3^{2k^2}\cdot3^{4k+2}=(8M+1)\,3^{4k+2}$, so
$3^{2(k+1)^2}-1=8M\cdot3^{4k+2}+\left(3^{4k+2}-1\right)$.
Now $3^{4k+2}-1=9\cdot81^k-1=9\left(81^k-1\right)+8$. Since $81^k-1=(81-1)\left(81^{k-1}+\dots+1\right)$ is divisible by $80$, hence by $8$, the term $3^{4k+2}-1$ is divisible by $8$.
So $3^{2(k+1)^2}-1$ is divisible by $8$, and by induction the result holds for all $n\ge1$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: The three positive numbers $r$, $s$ and $t$ are such that $(r+n)(s+n)(t+n)=n^6$. Given $(a+b+c)^3\ge27abc$ for any three positive real numbers $a,b,c$, show that $rst\le(n^2-n)^3$.
questions.answer:
Expanding: $rst+n(rs+st+tr)+n^2(r+s+t)+n^3=n^6$. (1)
Applying the given result to $r,s,t$: $r+s+t\ge3(rst)^{1/3}$. (2)
Applying it to $rs,st,tr$: $(rs+st+tr)^3\ge27(rs)(st)(tr)=27(rst)^2$, so $rs+st+tr\ge3(rst)^{2/3}$. (3)
Substituting (2) and (3) into (1):
$n^6\ge rst+3n(rst)^{2/3}+3n^2(rst)^{1/3}+n^3=\left[(rst)^{1/3}+n\right]^3$.
Taking cube roots: $(rst)^{1/3}+n\le n^2\Rightarrow(rst)^{1/3}\le n^2-n\Rightarrow rst\le(n^2-n)^3$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Consider $S_n=1+z+z^2+z^3+\dots+z^n$, where $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Show that $S_n=\dfrac{\operatorname{cis}((n+1)\theta)-1}{\operatorname{cis}\theta-1}$.
questions.answer: $S_n$ is a geometric series with first term $1$, common ratio $z$ and $n+1$ terms: $S_n=\dfrac{z^{n+1}-1}{z-1}$. By de Moivre's theorem $z^{n+1}=\operatorname{cis}((n+1)\theta)$, so $S_n=\dfrac{\operatorname{cis}((n+1)\theta)-1}{\operatorname{cis}\theta-1}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: With $S_n=1+z+\dots+z^n=\dfrac{\operatorname{cis}((n+1)\theta)-1}{\operatorname{cis}\theta-1}$ where $z=\operatorname{cis}\theta$, hence show that $\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\sin3\theta+\dots+\sin n\theta=\dfrac{\sin\!\left(\frac{n\theta}2\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{n+1}2\theta\right)}{\sin\!\left(\frac\theta2\right)}$.
questions.answer:
$\sin\theta+\dots+\sin n\theta=\operatorname{Im}(S_n)$, since $\operatorname{Im}(z^k)=\sin k\theta$ and $\operatorname{Im}(1)=0$.
Factor half-angles: for any $\varphi$, $\operatorname{cis}\varphi-1=\operatorname{cis}\frac\varphi2\left(\operatorname{cis}\frac\varphi2-\operatorname{cis}\!\left(-\frac\varphi2\right)\right)=\operatorname{cis}\frac\varphi2\cdot2i\sin\frac\varphi2$. So
$$S_n=\frac{\operatorname{cis}\frac{(n+1)\theta}2\cdot2i\sin\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\operatorname{cis}\frac\theta2\cdot2i\sin\frac\theta2}=\operatorname{cis}\frac{n\theta}2\cdot\frac{\sin\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$$
Taking the imaginary part: $\operatorname{Im}(S_n)=\sin\frac{n\theta}2\cdot\dfrac{\sin\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Let $\alpha$ be the complex number plotted on the Argand diagram below. Which expression is equal to $(\overline{\alpha})^{-1}$?
questions.answer: From the diagram $\alpha=2\operatorname{cis}\frac{2\pi}{7}$, so $\overline\alpha=2\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)$ and $(\overline\alpha)^{-1}=\frac12\operatorname{cis}\frac{2\pi}{7}$ (C).

questions.question: A polynomial with positive integer coefficients has roots $2$ and $4-5i$. Which of the following must also be a root?
questions.answer: The coefficients are real, so by the conjugate root theorem $\overline{4-5i}=4+5i$ is also a root.

questions.question: Using a $t$-substitution, which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1-\sin x-\cos x}$?
questions.answer: With $t=\tan\frac x2$, $dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$ and $1-\sin x-\cos x=\frac{(1+t^2)-2t-(1-t^2)}{1+t^2}=\frac{2t^2-2t}{1+t^2}$. So the integral is $\int\frac{2\,dt}{2t^2-2t}=\int\frac{dt}{t^2-t}$.

questions.question: If $|z|=1$ and $w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$ (where $z\ne-1$), which of the following is equal to $\text{Re}(w)$?
questions.answer: $w=\dfrac{(z-1)(\overline z+1)}{|z+1|^2}=\dfrac{|z|^2+z-\overline z-1}{|z+1|^2}=\dfrac{2i\,\text{Im}(z)}{|z+1|^2}$, which is purely imaginary, so $\text{Re}(w)=0$.

questions.question: A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $a=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}}$ m/s². It is initially at the origin, moving to the right at 2 m/s. At what position will it first reach a speed of 4 m/s?
questions.answer: $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=(x+1)^{-1/2}\Rightarrow\left[\tfrac12v^2\right]_2^4=\left[2\sqrt{x+1}\right]_0^x\Rightarrow 6=2\sqrt{x+1}-2\Rightarrow x=15$.

questions.question: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion with a period of $T$ seconds. At time $t=0$ it is at its centre of motion. Which of the following would be the best graph of $v^2$ against time?
questions.answer: At the centre the speed is greatest, so $v^2$ is a maximum at $t=0$. It is zero a quarter period later (an extremity) and a maximum again after half a period. This is graph B.

questions.question:
$\omega$ is a non-real cube root of unity and $n$ is an even positive integer. Evaluate
$$(1+\omega)(1+\omega^2)(1+\omega^4)(1+\omega^8)\cdots\left(1+\omega^{2^n}\right).$$
questions.answer: $\omega^{2^k}$ is $\omega$ for even $k$ and $\omega^2$ for odd $k$. Each pair $(1+\omega)(1+\omega^2)=2+\omega+\omega^2=1$. There are $n+1$ factors, so one unpaired factor $1+\omega=-\omega^2=-\dfrac1\omega$ remains.

questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ with $\text{Im}(\alpha)=\text{Im}(\beta)$ and $\text{Re}(\alpha)>\text{Re}(\beta)$. Which of the following equations can be used to find the set of values of $z$ where $\text{Arg}(z-\alpha)=2\,\text{Arg}(z-\beta)$?
questions.answer: In the triangle with vertices $z,\alpha,\beta$, the exterior angle at $\alpha$ is twice the interior angle at $\beta$, so the angle at $z$ equals the angle at $\beta$. The triangle is isosceles: $|z-\alpha|=|\beta-\alpha|$. (Equivalently, the angle at the centre $\alpha$ is twice the angle at the circumference.)

questions.question: Let $z=5-12i$ and $w=3+4i$. Find $v$ such that $3\overline v=z-2\overline w$.
questions.answer:
$$3\overline v=5-12i-2(3-4i)=-1-4i$$
Taking conjugates, $3v=-1+4i$, so $v=-\dfrac13+\dfrac43i$.

questions.question: Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $$\frac{5x^2-9x+4}{(x-3)(x^2+2)}=\frac{A}{x-3}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+2}.$$
Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{5x^2-9x+4}{(x-3)(x^2+2)}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Using partial fractions,
$$\int\left(\frac{2}{x-3}+\frac{3x}{x^2+2}\right)dx=2\ln|x-3|+\frac32\ln(x^2+2)+C.$$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\cos^{-1}(2x)\,dx$.
questions.answer:
By parts with $u=\cos^{-1}2x$, $dv=dx$:
$$\int\cos^{-1}2x\,dx=x\cos^{-1}2x+\int\frac{2x}{\sqrt{1-4x^2}}\,dx=x\cos^{-1}2x-\frac12\sqrt{1-4x^2}+C.$$

questions.question: Find the value of $k\in\mathbb R$ so that the circle $|z-2-2i|=1$ meets the region $\left|\text{Arg}(z-k-i)-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right|\ge\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in exactly two points.
questions.answer:
The region is $\text{Arg}(z-k-i)\ge\frac\pi3$ or $\text{Arg}(z-k-i)\le0$. Its complement is the wedge $0<\text{Arg}(z-k-i)<\frac\pi3$ with vertex $A(k,1)$.

For exactly two common points the circle (centre $C(2,2)$, radius 1) must lie in the wedge and touch both boundary rays. It already touches $y=1$ at $B(2,1)$. For it also to touch the ray at angle $\frac\pi3$, $AC$ bisects the wedge, so $\angle BAC=\frac\pi6$ and
$$AB=\frac{BC}{\tan\frac\pi6}=\sqrt3.$$
Hence $k=2-\sqrt3$.

questions.question:
A 2 kg toy helicopter is low on battery and provides a thrust of 10 N upwards. It starts falling from rest, and is subject to gravity and air resistance numerically equal to $kv^2$ where $k=0.096$. Take $g=9.8$ m/s². Let $x$ be the downward displacement (in metres) of the helicopter from its initial position, with velocity $v$ m/s and acceleration $a$ m/s².

Explain why the motion of the helicopter follows $a=4.8-0.048v^2$.
questions.answer:
Taking downwards as positive, the forces are weight $2g$ (down), thrust 10 N (up) and resistance $0.096v^2$ (up). By Newton's second law
$$2a=2(9.8)-10-0.096v^2\;\Rightarrow\;a=4.8-0.048v^2.$$

questions.question:
A 2 kg toy helicopter is low on battery and provides a thrust of 10 N upwards. It starts falling from rest, and is subject to gravity and air resistance numerically equal to $kv^2$ where $k=0.096$. Take $g=9.8$ m/s². Let $x$ be the downward displacement (in metres) of the helicopter from its initial position, with velocity $v$ m/s and acceleration $a$ m/s². Its motion satisfies $a=4.8-0.048v^2$.

Prove that the velocity of the helicopter is given by $v=\dfrac{10\left(e^{0.96t}-1\right)}{e^{0.96t}+1}$.
questions.answer:
$$\frac{dv}{dt}=0.048(100-v^2)\Rightarrow\int_0^v\frac{dv}{100-v^2}=0.048\int_0^t dt$$
$$\frac1{20}\int_0^v\left(\frac1{10-v}+\frac1{10+v}\right)dv=0.048t\Rightarrow\ln\frac{10+v}{10-v}=0.96t\quad(0\le v<10).$$
So $10+v=(10-v)e^{0.96t}$, giving $v\left(e^{0.96t}+1\right)=10\left(e^{0.96t}-1\right)$ and hence
$$v=\frac{10(e^{0.96t}-1)}{e^{0.96t}+1}.$$

Take $g=9.8$ m/s². Let $x$ be the downward displacement (in metres) of the helicopter from its initial position, with velocity $v$ m/s and acceleration $a$ m/s². Its motion satisfies $a=4.8-0.048v^2$.

Given that the helicopter hits the ground with speed 6.5 m/s, find the height it was initially at, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.answer:
$$v\frac{dv}{dx}=0.048(100-v^2)\Rightarrow\int_0^v\frac{v\,dv}{100-v^2}=0.048x\Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{0.096}\ln\frac{100}{100-v^2}=\frac{125}{12}\ln\frac{100}{100-v^2}.$$
At $v=6.5$: $x=\dfrac{125}{12}\ln\dfrac{100}{57.75}\approx5.72$ m.

*Note: the school's working uses $a=\frac{12}{125}(100-v^2)$ (twice the correct coefficient $\frac6{125}$), which would give 2.86 m; its stated answer of 5.72 m is nevertheless correct.*

questions.question: Using De Moivre's theorem, prove that $\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1$.
questions.answer:
Let $c=\cos\theta$, $s=\sin\theta$. By De Moivre, $\cos6\theta+i\sin6\theta=(c+is)^6$. Equating real parts of the binomial expansion:
$$\cos6\theta=c^6-15c^4s^2+15c^2s^4-s^6.$$
With $s^2=1-c^2$:
$$=c^6-15c^4(1-c^2)+15c^2(1-c^2)^2-(1-c^2)^3$$
$$=32c^6-48c^4+18c^2-1.$$

questions.question: Using the identity $\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1$ and a substitution $x=A\cos\theta$ for a suitable $A$, or otherwise, find all the roots of $P(x)=x^6-6x^4+9x^2-2$.
questions.answer:
Put $x=2\cos\theta$:
$$P(2\cos\theta)=64c^6-96c^4+36c^2-2=2(32c^6-48c^4+18c^2-1)=2\cos6\theta.$$
$\cos6\theta=0$ gives $\theta=\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{3\pi}{12},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{7\pi}{12},\frac{9\pi}{12},\frac{11\pi}{12}$, giving six distinct values of $2\cos\theta$. The roots are
$$x=\pm2\cos\frac{\pi}{12},\quad\pm\sqrt2,\quad\pm2\cos\frac{5\pi}{12}.$$

questions.question: A ball moves in a straight line according to $v^2=9(12+4x-x^2)$, where $v$ is its velocity in cm/s and $x$ is its displacement from the origin in cm. Prove that the ball is moving in simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer:
$$a=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=\frac92(4-2x)=-3^2(x-2),$$
which has the form $a=-n^2(x-c)$ with $n=3$, $c=2$. So the motion is simple harmonic.

questions.question: A ball moves in a straight line according to $v^2=9(12+4x-x^2)$, where $v$ is its velocity in cm/s and $x$ is its displacement from the origin in cm. Find the range of values of $x$ in which the ball can move.
questions.answer: $v^2\ge0\Rightarrow-9(x-6)(x+2)\ge0\Rightarrow-2\le x\le6$.

questions.question: A ball moves in a straight line according to $v^2=9(12+4x-x^2)$, where $v$ is its velocity in cm/s and $x$ is its displacement from the origin in cm. The ball is in the *extreme zone* when it is more than 2 cm from its central position. It completes one whole oscillation. For what percentage of the time, to the nearest whole number, is it in the extreme zone?
questions.answer:
The centre is $x=2$, the amplitude is 4 and $n=3$, so take $x=2+4\sin3t$ (period $\frac{2\pi}3$).

The extreme zone is $|x-2|>2$, i.e. $|\sin3t|>\frac12$. In one period $3t$ runs over $[0,2\pi]$ and this holds for $\frac\pi6<3t<\frac{5\pi}6$ and $\frac{7\pi}6<3t<\frac{11\pi}6$, a total of $\frac{4\pi}3$ out of $2\pi$.

The percentage is $\frac23\approx67\%$.

questions.question: By considering the expansion of $(z+1)^4$, or otherwise, solve $z^4+4z^3+8z^2+8z+3=0$.

Two weights of mass $m$ kg and $M$ kg are joined by a string of negligible mass over a smooth pulley at the top of a slope, as shown: $M$ lies on the slope and $m$ hangs vertically. The angle between the slope and the vertical is $\alpha$. A frictional force $F=\mu N$ acts on the mass $M$, where $N$ is the normal reaction of the slope on it and $\mu$ is a constant. The $m$ kg mass is moving downwards. By resolving parallel and perpendicular to the slope, show that the acceleration of the masses is $a=\dfrac{g(m-\mu M\sin\alpha-M\cos\alpha)}{m+M}$.
questions.answer:
For the hanging mass: $ma=mg-T$. (1)

For $M$ (friction acts down the slope since $M$ moves up), perpendicular to the slope: $N=Mg\sin\alpha$. Parallel to the slope:
$$Ma=T-Mg\cos\alpha-\mu N=T-Mg\cos\alpha-\mu Mg\sin\alpha.\quad(2)$$
Adding (1) and (2): $(m+M)a=g(m-M\cos\alpha-\mu M\sin\alpha)$, so
$$a=\frac{g(m-\mu M\sin\alpha-M\cos\alpha)}{m+M}.$$

questions.question: Two weights of mass $m$ kg and $M$ kg are joined by a string of negligible mass over a smooth pulley at the top of a slope, as shown: $M$ lies on the slope and $m$ hangs vertically. The angle between the slope and the vertical is $\alpha$. A frictional force $F=\mu N$ acts on the mass $M$, where $N$ is the normal reaction of the slope on it and $\mu$ is a constant. The $m$ kg mass is moving downwards with acceleration $a=\dfrac{g(m-\mu M\sin\alpha-M\cos\alpha)}{m+M}$. Find the tension in the string.
questions.answer: $$T=mg-ma=\frac{mg}{m+M}\left[m+M-m+\mu M\sin\alpha+M\cos\alpha\right]=\frac{mMg}{m+M}(1+\mu\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha).$$

The angle between the slope and the vertical is $\alpha$. A frictional force $F=\mu N$ acts on the mass $M$, where $N$ is the normal reaction of the slope on it and $\mu$ is a constant. The acceleration is $a=\dfrac{g(m-\mu M\sin\alpha-M\cos\alpha)}{m+M}$. Prove that if the vertically hung mass is moving downwards (accelerating from rest), then
$$\alpha<\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{m}{M\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right)-\tan^{-1}\frac1\mu.$$
You may assume that $\alpha+\tan^{-1}\dfrac1\mu<\dfrac\pi2$.
questions.answer:
We need $a>0$, i.e. $\dfrac mM>\mu\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha$.

Write $\mu\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha=R\sin(\alpha+\theta)$, with $R\cos\theta=\mu$ and $R\sin\theta=1$. So $R=\sqrt{1+\mu^2}$ and $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac1\mu$. Hence
$$\sin\left(\alpha+\tan^{-1}\tfrac1\mu\right)<\frac{m}{M\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}.$$
Since $0<\alpha+\tan^{-1}\frac1\mu<\frac\pi2$, where $\sin$ is increasing, (and provided the right side is at most 1, otherwise the inverse sine is undefined)
$$\alpha<\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{m}{M\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right)-\tan^{-1}\frac1\mu.$$

questions.question: A complex number $z$ satisfies $z^5+i=0$, where $z\ne-i$. Show that $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$.
questions.answer:
Since $i^5=i$, $z^5+i=z^5+i^5=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3+i^2z^2-i^3z+i^4)=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1)$.

This is zero and $z+i\ne0$, so $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$.

questions.question: A complex number $z$ satisfies $z^5+i=0$, where $z\ne-i$. Prove that $(z+i)\left(z^2+2iz\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{10}-1\right)=0$.
questions.answer:
$z^5=-i=\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac\pi2\right)$, so the roots are $z=\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{10}+\frac{2k\pi}{5}\right)$:
$$-i,\;\operatorname{cis}\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{10}\right),\;\operatorname{cis}\left(-\tfrac{9\pi}{10}\right),\;\operatorname{cis}\tfrac{3\pi}{10},\;\operatorname{cis}\tfrac{7\pi}{10}.$$
Pair the roots symmetric about the imaginary axis.

For $\operatorname{cis}(-\frac\pi{10}),\operatorname{cis}(-\frac{9\pi}{10})$: sum $=-2i\sin\frac\pi{10}$, product $=\operatorname{cis}(-\pi)=-1$, giving the factor $z^2+2iz\sin\frac\pi{10}-1$.

For $\operatorname{cis}\frac{3\pi}{10},\operatorname{cis}\frac{7\pi}{10}$: sum $=2i\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$, product $=\operatorname{cis}\pi=-1$, giving $z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1$.

Hence $z^5+i=(z+i)\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right)=0$.

questions.question: It is given that $$z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right).$$ Hence prove that $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}-\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{10}=-\dfrac12$.
questions.answer:
Equating coefficients of $z^3$:
$$2i\sin\frac\pi{10}-2i\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}=-i\;\Rightarrow\;\sin\frac\pi{10}-\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}=-\frac12.$$

For $\operatorname{cis}(-\frac\pi{10}),\operatorname{cis}(-\frac{9\pi}{10})$: sum $=-2i\sin\frac\pi{10}$, product $=\operatorname{cis}(-\pi)=-1$, giving the factor $z^2+2iz\sin\frac\pi{10}-1$.

For $\operatorname{cis}\frac{3\pi}{10},\operatorname{cis}\frac{7\pi}{10}$: sum $=2i\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$, product $=\operatorname{cis}\pi=-1$, giving $z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1$.

Hence $z^5+i=(z+i)\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right)=0$.

questions.question: It is given that $$z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right).$$ Hence find the exact values of $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}$ and $\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{10}$.
questions.answer:
Let $p=\sin\frac\pi{10}$, $q=\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$. Equating coefficients of $z^3$ gives $p-q=-\frac12$. Equating coefficients of $z^2$: $-2+4pq=-1$, so $pq=\frac14$.

With $q=p+\frac12$: $p\left(p+\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14\Rightarrow4p^2+2p-1=0\Rightarrow p=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{4}$.

Since $p>0$: $\sin\dfrac\pi{10}=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}$ and $\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{10}=\dfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}$.

prev.question: A complex number $z$ satisfies $z^5+i=0$, where $z\ne-i$. Show that $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$.
prev.answer:
Since $i^5=i$, $z^5+i=z^5+i^5=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3+i^2z^2-i^3z+i^4)=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1)$.

This is zero and $z+i\ne0$, so $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$.

questions.question: Let $\displaystyle I_n=\int_0^{\frac12}x^2(1-x^3)^n\,dx$ for $n\ge0$. Prove that $(k+1)I_k-kI_{k-1}=\dfrac1{24}\left(\dfrac78\right)^k$ for $k\ge1$.
questions.answer:
By parts with $u=(1-x^3)^k$, $dv=x^2dx$:
$$I_k=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}(1-x^3)^k\right]_0^{1/2}+k\int_0^{1/2}x^5(1-x^3)^{k-1}dx=\frac1{24}\left(\frac78\right)^k+k\int_0^{1/2}x^5(1-x^3)^{k-1}dx.$$
Write $x^5=x^2\left[1-(1-x^3)\right]$:
$$I_k=\frac1{24}\left(\frac78\right)^k+k\left(I_{k-1}-I_k\right).$$
Hence $(k+1)I_k-kI_{k-1}=\dfrac1{24}\left(\dfrac78\right)^k$.

questions.question:
Let $\displaystyle I_n=\int_0^{\frac12}x^2(1-x^3)^n\,dx$ for $n\ge0$. Using $(k+1)I_k-kI_{k-1}=\dfrac1{24}\left(\dfrac78\right)^k$ (for $k\ge1$) and taking an appropriate sum on both sides, prove that for all $n\ge0$,
$$I_n=\frac{1}{3(n+1)}\left[1-\left(\frac78\right)^{n+1}\right].$$
questions.answer:
Sum from $k=1$ to $n$. The left side telescopes to $(n+1)I_n-I_0$. The right side is a geometric series:
$$(n+1)I_n-I_0=\frac1{24}\cdot\frac{\frac78\left(1-(\frac78)^n\right)}{1-\frac78}=\frac7{24}\left(1-\left(\tfrac78\right)^n\right).$$
Now $I_0=\int_0^{1/2}x^2dx=\frac1{24}$, so
$$(n+1)I_n=\frac1{24}+\frac7{24}-\frac7{24}\left(\tfrac78\right)^n=\frac13\left[1-\left(\tfrac78\right)^{n+1}\right],$$
giving the result (it also holds for $n=0$).

questions.question: Prove that $\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^{\frac a2}\big[f(x)+f(a-x)\big]dx$.
questions.answer:
$$\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^{a/2}f(x)\,dx+\int_{a/2}^af(x)\,dx.$$
In the second integral put $x=a-u$, $dx=-du$:
$$\int_{a/2}^af(x)\,dx=-\int_{a/2}^0f(a-u)\,du=\int_0^{a/2}f(a-u)\,du,$$
and $u$ is a dummy variable. Adding gives the result.

questions.question: Let $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\ln(\sin x)\,dx$. Using $\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^{a/2}\big[f(x)+f(a-x)\big]dx$, or otherwise, prove that $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\frac\pi4}\ln\left(\frac{\sin2x}{2}\right)dx$.
questions.answer:
With $a=\frac\pi2$:
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\left[\ln\sin x+\ln\sin\left(\tfrac\pi2-x\right)\right]dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(\sin x\cos x)\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln\left(\frac{\sin2x}{2}\right)dx.$$

questions.question: Let $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\ln(\sin x)\,dx$. It is known that $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\frac\pi4}\ln\left(\frac{\sin2x}{2}\right)dx$. Hence evaluate $I$.
questions.answer:
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(\sin2x)\,dx-\frac\pi4\ln2.$$
With $u=2x$: $\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(\sin2x)\,dx=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin u)\,du=\frac I2$. So $I=\frac I2-\frac\pi4\ln2$, giving
$$I=-\frac\pi2\ln2.$$

questions.question: Seven distinct colours are used to colour the numbered sectors of a circle divided into $n$ sectors, as shown. Let $a_n$ be the number of ways to colour the circle so that each sector has one colour and any two adjacent sectors have different colours. Explain why $a_n+a_{n-1}=7\times6^{n-1}$ for integers $n\ge3$.
questions.answer:
Colour sector 1 (7 ways), then each of sectors $2,3,\dots,n$ differently from the one before it (6 ways each). This gives $7\times6^{n-1}$ colourings in which every adjacent pair differs, except possibly sectors $n$ and 1.

These split into two cases:
- sector $n$ differs from sector 1: a valid colouring of $n$ sectors, $a_n$ ways;
- sector $n$ has the same colour as sector 1: merge sectors $n$ and 1 into one sector. This gives exactly a valid colouring of a circle with $n-1$ sectors, $a_{n-1}$ ways.

Hence $a_n+a_{n-1}=7\times6^{n-1}$.

questions.question:
Seven distinct colours are used to colour the numbered sectors of a circle divided into $n$ sectors, as shown. Let $a_n$ be the number of ways to colour the circle so that each sector has one colour and any two adjacent sectors have different colours. It is known that $a_n+a_{n-1}=7\times6^{n-1}$ for $n\ge3$, and that $a_2=42$. Use mathematical induction to show that for integers $n\ge3$,
$$a_n=6\times(-1)^n+6^n.$$
questions.answer:
**$n=3$:** three mutually adjacent sectors give $a_3=7\times6\times5=210$, and $6(-1)^3+6^3=-6+216=210$. True.

**Assume** $a_k=6(-1)^k+6^k$ for some $k\ge3$.

**$n=k+1$:**
$$a_{k+1}=7\times6^k-a_k=7\times6^k-6^k-6(-1)^k=6^{k+1}+6(-1)^{k+1}.$$
So the result is true for $k+1$, and by induction for all $n\ge3$.

questions.question: A 100 g football is kicked up a slope with equation $2y-x=0$, from the origin $O$, with speed $25\sqrt2$ m/s at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal. It is subject to gravity ($10$ m/s²) and air resistance $-0.02\mathbf v$ newtons, where $\mathbf v$ is its velocity, so its acceleration is $\mathbf a=-\mathbf g-0.2\mathbf v$, where $\mathbf g=\begin{pmatrix}0\\10\end{pmatrix}$. Show that the vertical displacement of the football is $y=-50t+375\left(1-e^{-0.2t}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Vertically $\dfrac{dv_y}{dt}=-10-0.2v_y=-\tfrac15(50+v_y)$, with $v_y(0)=25\sqrt2\sin45^\circ=25$.
$$\int_{25}^{v_y}\frac{dv}{50+v}=-\frac t5\Rightarrow\ln\frac{50+v_y}{75}=-0.2t\Rightarrow v_y=75e^{-0.2t}-50.$$
Integrating with $y(0)=0$:
$$y=-375e^{-0.2t}-50t+375=-50t+375(1-e^{-0.2t}).$$

questions.question: A 100 g football is kicked up a slope with equation $2y-x=0$, from the origin $O$, with speed $25\sqrt2$ m/s at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal. It is subject to gravity ($10$ m/s²) and air resistance $-0.02\mathbf v$ newtons, where $\mathbf v$ is its velocity, so its acceleration is $\mathbf a=-\mathbf g-0.2\mathbf v$, where $\mathbf g=\begin{pmatrix}0\\10\end{pmatrix}$. Prove that the Cartesian equation of the trajectory is $y=3x+250\ln\left(1-\dfrac{x}{125}\right)$.

questions.question: A football kicked from the origin up the slope $2y-x=0$ follows the trajectory $y=3x+250\ln\left(1-\dfrac{x}{125}\right)$. The graph below shows the point where $y=5$ on the curve $y=\dfrac{4\ln(1+x)}{x}$: it is $(-0.37137,\,5)$. Hence, or otherwise, find the range $R$ of the kick, measured up the slope, correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.answer:
The ball lands where $3x+250\ln\left(1-\frac{x}{125}\right)=\frac x2$, i.e. $250\ln\left(1-\frac x{125}\right)=-\frac{5x}{2}$.

Let $z=-\frac{x}{125}$, so $x=-125z$:
$$250\ln(1+z)=\frac{625z}{2}\Rightarrow\frac{4\ln(1+z)}{z}=5.$$
From the graph $z=-0.37137$, so $x=125\times0.37137=46.42125$.

On the slope $y=\frac x2$, so
$$R=\sqrt{x^2+\left(\tfrac x2\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}x\approx51.9005\text{ m}.$$

questions.question: Explain why $\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}\left[\int_0^{g(x)}h(t)\,dt\right]=g'(x)\,h(g(x))$.
questions.answer:
Let $H$ be a primitive of $h$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus the integral equals $H(g(x))-H(0)$. Differentiating by the chain rule ($H(0)$ is constant):
$$H'(g(x))\,g'(x)=g'(x)\,h(g(x)).$$

questions.question: Consider the area under the graph $y=\sqrt{1+t^2}$ between $t=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x}$ and $t=\sqrt x$, where $x>0$. Using $\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}\left[\int_0^{g(x)}h(t)\,dt\right]=g'(x)\,h(g(x))$, find the value of $x$ for which the area is minimised.
questions.answer:
$$A(x)=\int_0^{\sqrt x}\sqrt{1+t^2}\,dt-\int_0^{-1/\sqrt x}\sqrt{1+t^2}\,dt.$$
Here $\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt x=\frac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\left(-x^{-1/2}\right)=\frac12x^{-3/2}$, so
$$A'(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+x}}{2\sqrt x}-\frac{1}{2x\sqrt x}\sqrt{1+\frac1x}=\frac{\sqrt{1+x}}{2\sqrt x}-\frac{\sqrt{1+x}}{2x^2}=\frac{\sqrt{1+x}}{2x^2}\left(x^{3/2}-1\right).$$
For $x>0$, $A'(x)=0$ only at $x=1$, with $A'<0$ for $x<1$ and $A'>0$ for $x>1$. So the area is a minimum when $x=1$.

questions.question: A circle centred at $P$ is inscribed in a right-angled triangle $OVW$ (right angle at $O$), touching the sides at $S$ (on $OV$), $U$ (on $OW$) and $Q$ (on the hypotenuse $VW$), as shown. $\overrightarrow{VQ}=k\overrightarrow{VW}$ with $k>0$. Let $\overrightarrow{OS}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OU}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{OV}=\mu\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OW}=\lambda\mathbf b$, where $\lambda,\mu>1$. Explain why $\overrightarrow{VQ}=k(\lambda\mathbf b-\mu\mathbf a)$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{VW}=\overrightarrow{OW}-\overrightarrow{OV}=\lambda\mathbf b-\mu\mathbf a$, so $\overrightarrow{VQ}=k\overrightarrow{VW}=k(\lambda\mathbf b-\mu\mathbf a)$.

questions.question: A circle centred at $P$ is inscribed in a right-angled triangle $OVW$ (right angle at $O$), touching the sides at $S$ (on $OV$), $U$ (on $OW$) and $Q$ (on the hypotenuse $VW$), as shown. $\overrightarrow{VQ}=k\overrightarrow{VW}$ with $k>0$. Let $\overrightarrow{OS}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OU}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{OV}=\mu\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OW}=\lambda\mathbf b$, where $\lambda,\mu>1$. By considering $VS$, prove that $k=\dfrac{\mu-1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+\mu^2}}$.
questions.answer:
$OSPU$ is a square with side equal to the radius $r$, so $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=r$, and $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=0$.

$\overrightarrow{SV}=(\mu-1)\mathbf a$, so $VS=(\mu-1)r$.

$VQ^2=k^2|\lambda\mathbf b-\mu\mathbf a|^2=k^2r^2(\lambda^2+\mu^2)$, so $VQ=kr\sqrt{\lambda^2+\mu^2}$.

Tangents from an external point are equal, $VS=VQ$, hence $k=\dfrac{\mu-1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+\mu^2}}$.

Given that $k=\dfrac{\mu-1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+\mu^2}}$ and $k=\dfrac{\lambda+\mu^2-\mu}{\lambda^2+\mu^2}$, prove that $\lambda=\dfrac{2(\mu-1)}{\mu-2}$.

$$\lambda^2(\mu-1)^2=\lambda^2+2\lambda\mu(\mu-1).$$
Since $\lambda\ne0$: $\lambda(\mu^2-2\mu)=2\mu(\mu-1)$, hence $\lambda=\dfrac{2(\mu-1)}{\mu-2}$.

questions.question: A circle centred at $P$ is inscribed in a right-angled triangle $OVW$ (right angle at $O$), touching the sides at $S$ (on $OV$), $U$ (on $OW$) and $Q$ (on the hypotenuse $VW$), as shown. $\overrightarrow{VQ}=k\overrightarrow{VW}$ with $k>0$. Let $\overrightarrow{OS}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OU}=\mathbf b$, $\overrightarrow{OV}=\mu\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OW}=\lambda\mathbf b$, where $\lambda,\mu>1$. Using these results, or otherwise, show that the area of the inscribed circle is $\dfrac\pi4(OV+OW-VW)^2$.
questions.answer:
Let $r$ be the radius. The triangle splits into $OPV$, $OPW$ and $VPW$, each with height $r$:
$$\tfrac12\,OV\cdot OW=\tfrac12r\,(OV+OW+VW)\Rightarrow r=\frac{OV\cdot OW}{OV+OW+VW}.$$
By Pythagoras, $(OV+OW)^2-VW^2=2\,OV\cdot OW$, i.e.
$$(OV+OW-VW)(OV+OW+VW)=2\,OV\cdot OW.$$
Therefore $r=\dfrac{OV+OW-VW}{2}$ and the area is
$$\pi r^2=\frac\pi4(OV+OW-VW)^2.$$

questions.question: What is the converse of the statement "if you can't see my mirrors, then I can't see you"?
questions.answer: The converse of $P\Rightarrow Q$ is $Q\Rightarrow P$: if I can't see you, then you can't see my mirrors.
options: If I can't see your mirrors, then you can't see me.
If I can't see you, then you can't see my mirrors.
If you can see me, then I can see your mirrors.
If I can see you, then you can see my mirrors.

questions.question: What is the contrapositive of the statement "if you can't see my mirrors, then I can't see you"?
questions.answer: The contrapositive of $P\Rightarrow Q$ is $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$: if I can see you, then you can see my mirrors.
options: If I can't see your mirrors, then you can't see me.
If I can't see you, then you can't see my mirrors.
If you can see me, then I can see your mirrors.
If I can see you, then you can see my mirrors.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ moves so that its velocity is $v=f(x)$. The resultant force causing this motion is:
questions.answer: $F=m\,v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=mf(x)f'(x)$.

questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a non-real cube root of unity. What is the value of $(1+2\omega+3\omega^2)(1+3\omega+2\omega^2)$?
questions.answer: Using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$ the product is $(\omega+2\omega^2)(2\omega+\omega^2)=2\omega^2+5\omega^3+2\omega^4=5+2(\omega^2+\omega)=3$.

questions.question: Suppose $z_1$ and $z_2$ are distinct non-zero complex numbers with $|z_1+z_2|=|z_1-z_2|$. Which of the following is always true?
questions.answer: The parallelogram on $z_1,z_2$ has equal diagonals, so it is a rectangle. Hence $\arg z_1-\arg z_2=\pm\frac\pi2$ and $\frac{z_1}{z_2}$ is purely imaginary.

questions.question: A particle moves from $t=t_0$, $x=x_0$, $v=v_0$ to $t=t_F$, $x=x_F$, $v=v_F$ with acceleration $\ddot x$. Which of the following is **incorrect**?
questions.answer: From $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=f(v)$, $x_F=\displaystyle\int_{v_0}^{v_F}\frac{v}{f(v)}\,dv+x_0$, so B has the integrand upside down.

questions.question: Suppose $a,b,c$ are non-zero real numbers with $\dfrac{a^2}{b^2+c^2}<\dfrac{b^2}{c^2+a^2}<\dfrac{c^2}{a^2+b^2}$. Which statement can be deduced?
questions.answer: Take reciprocals (reversing the inequalities) and add 1 to each: $\dfrac{S}{a^2}>\dfrac{S}{b^2}>\dfrac{S}{c^2}$ where $S=a^2+b^2+c^2$. So $a^2<b^2<c^2$.

questions.question: Give a counterexample to disprove: for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, if $x^2\ge y^2$ then $x\ge y$.
questions.answer: Take $x=-1$, $y=0$. Then $x^2=1\ge0=y^2$ but $x=-1<0=y$. So the statement is false.

questions.question: Write down the negation of: there exists $k\in\mathbb R$ such that $k^2<0$.
questions.answer: For all $k\in\mathbb R$, $k^2\ge0$.

questions.question: Using integration by parts, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}x\cos x\,dx$.
questions.answer: $$\big[x\sin x\big]_0^{\pi/2}-\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx=\frac\pi2+\big[\cos x\big]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac\pi2-1.$$

questions.question: Evaluate $\text{Arg}\left(i^{2025}\right)$, where $\text{Arg}(z)$ is the principal argument.
Find $\displaystyle\int\cos^3x\,\sin^2x\,dx$.
questions.answer: $$\int\sin^2x(1-\sin^2x)\cos x\,dx=\frac13\sin^3x-\frac15\sin^5x+C.$$

questions.question: By using an appropriate $t$-substitution, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\frac{d\theta}{3+2\cos4\theta}$.
questions.answer:
Let $t=\tan2\theta$, so $d\theta=\dfrac{dt}{2(1+t^2)}$ and $\cos4\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$.
$$\int\frac{dt}{2(1+t^2)\left(3+\frac{2(1-t^2)}{1+t^2}\right)}=\frac12\int\frac{dt}{t^2+5}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt5}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan2\theta}{\sqrt5}\right)+C.$$

questions.question: By expanding $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3$ and using de Moivre's theorem, show that $\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$.
questions.answer:
$(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos^3\theta+3i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-i\sin^3\theta$.

By de Moivre this equals $\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta$. Equating real parts:
$$\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta.$$

questions.question: Using $\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$, or otherwise, solve $8x^3-6x+1=0$ (let $x=\cos\theta$).
questions.answer:
With $x=\cos\theta$: $2(4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta)=-1$, so $\cos3\theta=-\frac12$.

$3\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3},\frac{8\pi}{3}$, giving $\theta=\frac{2\pi}9,\frac{4\pi}9,\frac{8\pi}9$. The three distinct roots are
$$x=\cos\frac{2\pi}9,\;\cos\frac{4\pi}9,\;\cos\frac{8\pi}9.$$

questions.question: The roots of $8x^3-6x+1=0$ are $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}9$, $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}9$ and $\cos\dfrac{8\pi}9$. Deduce that $\cos\dfrac\pi9-\cos\dfrac{2\pi}9-\cos\dfrac{4\pi}9=0$.
questions.answer:
The sum of the roots is $0$ (no $x^2$ term):
$$\cos\tfrac{2\pi}9+\cos\tfrac{4\pi}9+\cos\tfrac{8\pi}9=0.$$
Since $\cos\frac{8\pi}9=-\cos\frac\pi9$, this gives $\cos\frac\pi9-\cos\frac{2\pi}9-\cos\frac{4\pi}9=0$.

questions.question: Particles of mass 1 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. The 3 kg mass lies on a smooth plane inclined at $\theta$ to the horizontal and the 1 kg mass hangs vertically, as shown. Find $\theta$ (in degrees, to one decimal place) so that the system is in equilibrium.
questions.answer:
Hanging mass: $T=g$. Mass on the plane, along the plane: $T=3g\sin\theta$.

So $\sin\theta=\frac13$ and $\theta\approx19.5^\circ$.

questions.question: The velocity $v$ of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $v^2=12+8x-4x^2$, where $x$ is its displacement from $O$. Prove that the particle is undergoing simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: $$\ddot x=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=\frac{d}{dx}(6+4x-2x^2)=-4(x-1),$$ which is of the form $-n^2(x-c)$. So the motion is simple harmonic.

questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along the $x$-axis with $v^2=12+8x-4x^2$ (so $\ddot x=-4(x-1)$). Find the period, amplitude and centre of motion.
questions.answer:
$n=2$, so the period is $\pi$. The centre is $x=1$.

$v=0$ when $-4(x-3)(x+1)=0$, so the extremes are $x=-1,3$ and the amplitude is $2$.
